#1017. Wolff: 'Good person' Antonelli should be a role model for entitled F1 drivers

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff lauded Kimi Antonelli and stated the new world champion "represents the modern Formula 1 driver"; watch Friday's practice sessions at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix from 3.30pm and 7pm, live on Sky Sports F1

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Mercedes boss Toto Wolff says newly crowned world champion Kimi Antonelli should be a role model for both upcoming drivers and some of his “entitled” Formula 1 rivals.

The 20-year-old Italian become the sport's youngest ever world champion as he wrapped up the title with four rounds to spare at Sunday's Mexico City Grand Prix.

Antonelli has not only produced a historic campaign in just his second season in F1, but has also charmed his Mercedes colleagues, rivals, and fans with his charm and youthful exuberance.

At the end of his briefing with the written media in Mexico following the race, Wolff gave an unpromoted impassioned speech praising Antonelli.

"This notion of win at all costs, selfish, opportunistic, ruthless for your own benefit. That model of racing driver has died," Wolff said.

"We have a new champion that represents values - humility, integrity, loyalty, respect. Being himself. He should be a role model for many other young drivers in junior formulas.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"He should be a role model for the few entitled ones in Formula 1 - the endless moaners on the radio, the ones that complain, the ones that crash.

"Look at this kid of 20 years [old] and then think what you can do in order to improve. That's the message to these kids.

"That is how the FIA, that Mohammed [Ben Sulayem], that Stefano [Domenicali], that's how I would want to see racing drivers in the future.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"That is modern Formula 1. Kimi represents the modern Formula 1 driver because of those values, not only because of his talent.

"The talent is there with everyone. But you have got to be a good person too. He has demonstrated that you can beat everyone out there by being a good person."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Antonelli only needed to finish in the top nine in Mexico to seal the title, but produced a strong drive to finish on the podium behind race winner Max Verstappen, and Lewis Hamilton.

Hamilton shares the record for the most F1 titles on seven, while Verstappen has four, and after the race Antonelli appeared to already be thinking about joining them as multiple world champions.

Antonelli told Sky Sports F1: "This is just the beginning. This win is just going to mark a new beginning, a new point to build on to keep improving and to keep trying to win championships.

"Obviously it's been incredible to share the podium with Max and Lewis and hopefully there will be many more battles with them in the future."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Antonelli failed to meet expectations at times during his rookie campaign last season, with a poor run of results during the European summer leading many to question Mercedes' decision to fast-track him into one of the sport's most desirable seats after Hamilton's switch to Ferrari.

The Italian admitted he has enjoyed silencing his critics with his remarkable jump forward this season.

"It's always good to shut off some of the noise. Of course, I think in many ways it does help to add fuel to the fire, the fact that some people said that I wasn't belonging to Formula 1 or I wasn't ready for it, which, at some point last year, probably looked like that I wasn't ready for it," said Antonelli.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"But I think last year, being able to experience those moments made me much more ready as well ahead of this year. I think experiencing really low and difficult situations, high-pressure moments, really helped me to face certain situations this year, and definitely they made me mature a lot as a driver and as a person.

"And still this year, I've had moments where I could have done better, a lot better. So, yeah, it's just a constant learning process.

"But I think last year, being able to race straight into Mercedes, obviously straight under the spotlight, made me grow much, much faster than if I would have gone to a smaller team, for example."

The former USMNT international was heralded as the game’s next superstar when he was coming up through the ranks

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Freddy Adu was barely into his teenage years when the hype began.

Even before he made his senior debut at D.C. United as a 14-year-old, Adu was heralded as ‘the next Pele’ as he was talked up as not just a promising young player, but a generational talent who was being tipped for global stardom.

But compared to the Brazilian great at such a young age came with a weight of expectation that no child should have to even comprehend, let alone live up to. As Adu looks back at this career, he explains that the excitement of being compared to his idol would soon give way to the realisation that he needed to forge his own path.

Asked by FourFourTwo when he realised he might be destined for something special, Adu says: “When I was 11 or 12. My team, the Bethesda Internationals, were one of the top four teams in the nation and we were in the national championships.

“A lot of teams were playing, there were a bunch of fields, and when my team played, everybody – and I mean everybody, all the other parents, all the other teams – would come and gather around our field to watch.”

This was the first time that Adu had experienced this kind of attention, as his matches became must-watch affairs for local fans and players.

“They’d heard of this 11-year-old, and it was under 14s, so I was playing three years up. It was really cool – that was the first time I got a taste of pressure,” he continues.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

This excitement would grow, with Adu’s name going way past youth tournaments and into the mainstream media.

As a consequence of this, comparisons with Pele, Adu’s hero, began to emerge.

“As a kid, when I first heard it, I thought it was cool to be compared to your idol, because Pele was my idol,” Adu continues.

But eventually, the enormity of the situation would sink in and the comparison to the three-time World Cup winner and all-time great began to weigh on him.

“Then it set in that ‘Oh my God…’ It took a few months to realise ‘Alright, now you’ve really got to perform’, because people aren’t just comparing anybody to Pele. Then I started thinking ‘You can’t allow this to happen’.

“I had to say ‘Look, I’m my own player, you can’t compare me to one of the greatest players who ever played, I’m not him’. I had to come to terms with being my own player and just focus on being me, rather than being Pele.”

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Replacing a club legend is never easy, especially when overseeing a major squad rebuild. But despite losing key figures like Bruno Guimarães, Sandro Tonali, Anthony Gordon and Kieran Trippier, Matthias Jaissle has guided Newcastle United to eighth in the Premier League, two points behind fifth-placed Chelsea.

For a club that has played Champions League football in two of the last three seasons, expectations remain considerably higher. Newcastle's inconsistent results have raised questions about their progress under Jaissle, but beneath the surface, there are promising signs that the German is laying the bedrock for a new era.

Newcastle recorded the Premier League's sixth-best expected goals against (50.95) but conceded 55 goals last season, the sixth-worst tally in the division, and finished 12th. Jaissle initially struggled to address those weaknesses, conceding eight goals in his first four league matches and two against West Bromwich Albion in the EFL Cup.

However, the underlying numbers suggest a marked improvement. According to Gradient Sports, Newcastle ranked 19th in the Premier League for tackling and duel performance across the opening four weeks of the season. Over the next four weeks, they climbed to seventh and sixth, respectively, while their positioning ranking jumped from 13th to third.

Newcastle's center backs rose from 16th to eighth in average overall performance grade, their fullbacks from fourth to first, and their aerial duels from eighth to first. These upgrades suggest a more cohesive defensive unit, but individual shortcomings remain a concern: Sven Botman has committed a league-high five errors leading to shots this season.

"We are searching now for stabilisation" Matthias Jaissle speaks ahead of Newcastle's visit to Everton in the Carabao Cup! 🎙️ https://t.co/jNZtpCJ4MFOctober 29, 2026

There has been progress in midfield, too. With Guimarães and Tonali gone, Lewis Miley has assumed greater responsibility, improving his average grade by 11.15 points between the opening four weeks and the following four. Nico González's grade has also increased by 9.20 points over the same period.

But while Jaissle has improved the team's defense and midfield, attack is another story. Newcastle's wingers have dropped from ninth to 18th in average performance between the two four-week periods, while their center forwards climbed from 19th to 18th. Newcastle also rank 16th for expected goals per match and chance quality, and joint 13th for shots.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The successive departures of Alexander Isak and Gordon have deprived Newcastle of two major attacking weapons, and their replacements have struggled to fill the void. Jaissle has fortified their defensive base, but he has yet to develop an attacking structure capable of creating gilt-edged chances, and he is yet to find his strongest team.

Nevertheless, last weekend's trip to Crystal Palace offered plenty of reason for optimism. After three defeats in four matches, Jaissle made five changes to his starting XI, replacing Botman and Malick Thiaw with Dan Burn and Fabian Schär, while restoring Amar Dedić, Jacob Murphy and William Osula to the lineup.

These changes paid dividends. Burn and Schär helped the Magpies secure their first clean sheet in two months, while Murphy and Dedić assisted goals for Osula and Harvey Barnes. And instead of dropping between the center backs, González operated further forward and was more involved in Newcastle's attacking buildup.

After a subdued first half, Newcastle showed more urgency in exploiting turnovers and scored twice in the first 13 minutes after the restart. It offered a glimpse of what they could look like if Jaissle can fix an attack that has been declining since Eddie Howe's last year in charge. However, Thursday's defeat to Everton served as a reminder of the inconsistency that continues to plague their growth.

Unlike at Red Bull Salzburg and Al-Ahli, where he enjoyed substantial financial backing and squads capable of competing for silverware, Jaissle is now overseeing a Newcastle team in transition. With several established starters gone and their replacements still finding their feet, this is undoubtedly a work in progress.

It would be premature to call the Palace victory a turning point, but the data suggests that Jaissle is gradually building a stronger foundation. Whether they can translate that progress into a sustained push for European qualification will depend on solving the problem that has persisted throughout his tenure: making Newcastle lethal in the final third.

Fluent in Spanish, Portuguese and Italian, Lowy’s versatile skillset has allowed him to traverse a number of different fields when covering major competitions like the FIFA Club World Cup. In addition to football, he is also a seasoned participant of other sports like pickleball, tennis, and volleyball.

#1011. Mikel Arteta confirms huge William Saliba injury boost for Arsenal

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Defender Saliba hasn’t played for Arsenal this season due to a back injury but was spotted in training on Tuesday and Arteta says he is fit once more

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Mikel Arteta has confirmed that William Saliba is fit and ready to return to the Arsenal line-up in a huge boost for the Gunners.

Centre-back Saliba was a key cog in Arsenal’s Premier League title win last term but has not played this season due to a back injury that he sustained during the World Cup this summer.

Summer signing Ezri Konsa has been hugely impressive as a replacement for the Frenchman – forming a formidable partnership with Gabriel in the heart of the Gunners defence – but Saliba was spotted back in first-team training on Tuesday morning.

Arsenal face Slavia Prague in the Champions League on Wednesday and in his pre-match press conference, Arteta confirmed the 25-year-old is fit once more and successfully came through a behind-closed-doors friendly without any setbacks.

“He’s in a really good place,” said Arteta. “The process and the timings and the manner that the injury has been dealt with, especially the feelings that Willy has been having along the way, they have been very, very positive.

“His evolution has been as expected, which is not always the case. He feels really comfortable.

“He played 45 minutes behind closed doors last week. He feels ready to go. Whether we use him or not now is a matter of what the team needs.”

Arsenal produced a defensive masterclass to win at Anfield for the first time in 14 years at the weekend, beating Liverpool 1-0, and have kept four clean sheets in a row in the Premier League.

It is presumed that Saliba won’t be rushed back after such an extended injury lay-off but Arteta hinted that he wouldn’t necessarily limit the defender’s minutes to ease him in.

“Now you’re in or not,” added the Spaniard. “Now he’s in. He’s in like anybody else. All the preparation has been done to make sure all the load and all the steps have been done to minimise the risk.

“He’s in a really good place, he’s built the capacity that we needed. Now it’s about giving him minutes.

“He’s a centre-back. When that’s the case, it’s not like an attacking midfielder or a No 9 you can change. A centre-back normally has to be able to play 90 minutes. That’s why all the preparation that we have done to build him.”

The return of Saliba will offer Arteta a selection headache, with Konsa having settled in so well at the Emirates Stadium.

The England international could theoretically slide across to right-back to accommodate the Frenchman in the first-choice starting line-up and the Gunners boss is excited to have more options at his disposal.

“So far we haven’t had that luxury – I wouldn’t call it a problem,” Arteta said. “The moment they are fit and available, we’re going to have opportunities to load the players and manage their congestion in a better way than we’ve done it.

“Ezri can play as a full-back. I think his main position is centre-back. He can play right or left, Willy has done the same with the national team and here at Arsenal. That’s going to be something really positive for the team.”

#1009. Nature awards recognize inspiring women in science

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

This year, the Nature Awards for Inspiring Women in Science recognized Taghried Abdelmagid (left) in the Science Outreach category and Alexandra Paterson in the Science Achievement category.Credit: Courtesy of Taghried Isam Abdel-Magid (left); Brad Nally, UK College of Engineering/University of Kentucky (right)

Every year, we remind the research community that women’s contributions to science need to be better recognized and rewarded. The importance of this was underlined only last month, when 2026 became another year in which no women were awarded a Nobel prize in the sciences or economics. The Nature Awards for Inspiring Women in Science, a partnership with the Estée Lauder Companies, are intended to help bend the curve of recognition. Given the awards’ focus on women in the early stages of their careers, they are also intended to create a legacy that will benefit others for many years to come.

Nature’s Inspiring Women in Science Awards

Nature’s Inspiring Women in Science Awards

Alexandra Paterson, the winner of this year’s Scientific Achievement award, is a materials physicist at the University of Kentucky in Lexington, and originally from the United Kingdom. She has been recognized for, among other things, groundbreaking work in developing semiconductors from flexible polymer-based materials. These semiconductors, known as plastic mixed conductors, have potential applications in technologies ranging from cardiovascular sensors to low-energy computing.

Unlike most conventional semiconductors, plastic mixed conductors are made from mechanically flexible materials and can be manufactured using low-cost printing. Researchers have struggled with the stability of these conductors, which often do not last long or perform reliably. However, last year, Paterson and her colleagues showed that stability could be improved by using a new materials-engineering technique (V. N. Le et al. Nature Electron. 8, 116–126; 2025).

Celebrate women in research and the networks that sustain them

Celebrate women in research and the networks that sustain them

Our second winner, Taghried Abdelmagid, is at the University of Bath, UK, where she studies sustainability in construction materials. Originally from Sudan, her award, which is in the Science Outreach category, recognizes her part in a female volunteer-led initiative called Share the Knowledge–Sudan (StK). This provides training and mentoring to people — most of them women — in Sudan and in the Sudanese diaspora, so that they can embark on or continue to pursue research careers.

Sudan is experiencing what is often described as the world’s worst humanitarian crisis. Since armed conflict broke out in 2023, some 14 million people have been displaced, either within the country or to neighbouring countries, including Egypt, Ethiopia, South Sudan and Uganda. The United Nations estimated in August that hundreds of thousands of people have lost their lives.

Many of Sudan’s universities have also been destroyed. Abdelmagid and her colleagues established StK in an effort to ensure that girls and women — whose education is often disproportionately affected by conflict — can continue to access scientific knowledge, along with expertise, training and mentorship. StK provides a range of online services, such as talks from scientists, which can attract up to 1,500 attendees, and access to a free digital library. For those pursuing or planning research careers, there is coaching and mentoring, support with developing research proposals and help with interview preparation.

Many research awards, not least the Nobel prizes, are designed to recognize individual achievement. Doing so is important, to ensure that appropriate credit is apportioned for discoveries and inventions.

Women need platforms to celebrate excellence in research and technology

Women need platforms to celebrate excellence in research and technology

But scientific awards should also seek to recognize and celebrate shared endeavours, including collaborations that cross borders and disciplines. Paterson’s work, for example, requires knowledge of polymer chemistry, electronics and biotechnology, and her team is involved in collaborations with institutions spread across three continents.

Many of those shortlisted for this week’s Nature Awards have gone above and beyond to foster collaboration and teamwork, and are using their talents, skills and networks to make science accessible to those who would otherwise struggle to study or secure careers in science.

Paterson was raised in the town of Oldham in the north of England, a region affected by some of the country’s highest levels of deprivation. Kentucky, where she is now based, is one of the most deprived US states, and Paterson is involved in a project to establish a materials-science exhibition at the Lexington Children’s Museum.

Other women recognized in this year’s awards include Rose Huizenga, the runner-up in the Science Outreach category, who founded Coral Catch, a women-led marine conservation organization based in Indonesia.

Diversify Nobel-prize nominations before it’s too late

Diversify Nobel-prize nominations before it’s too late

Nandintsetseg Dejid, the runner-up in the Scientific Achievement category, studies land-migrating animals in Central Asia. She is based at the Senckenberg Biodiversity and Climate Research Centre in Frankfurt, Germany.

And Victoria Peterson, a biomedical engineer at the Institute of Applied Mathematics of the Litoral in Santa Fe, Argentina, received a special judges’ commendation for her study of brain–computer interfaces for neurorehabilitation and for her commitment to empowering the next generation of researchers in her field across Latin America.

We’re proud of our winners, those shortlisted, and all that they embody. We wish them, and everyone nominated, the very best, and look forward to seeing them flourish.

#1008. Enzo Maresca speaks out on Man City's reliance on Erling Haaland after Premier League setbacks

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Manchester City have lost their last two Premier League games to fall behind Arsenal in the table

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Enzo Maresca has warned his Manchester City squad that they cannot simply rely on Erling Haaland for goals after losing their last two Premier League games.

The striker failed to find the net on Saturday as City lost 1-0 at Brighton, and that defeat cost the team their place at the top of the Premier League as Arsenal took full advantage by beating Liverpool the following day.

City were also beaten 2-1 by Aston Villa prior to the Brighton loss, and Maresca believes it is essential that other players begin adding to the goals tally to help Haaland.

The City manager said: “It’s very important that in each game, we created chances. For sure, when you have Erling inside the pitch, it’s better because he’s going to score goals, or you know he’s always there close.

“At the same time, we cannot rely on Erling for every game. We need also the rest to score goals.

“But, again, I think the last game against Brighton was the only game of the season where we didn’t score. But, for sure, if Erling is on the pitch we are happy.”

Maresca was speaking to media in Germany ahead of City’s Champions League league phase match against RB Leipzig on Wednesday.

City have made a solid start in the competition, with victories over Porto and AEK Athens. The one setback came last month, when they were beaten by holders PSG.

Phil Foden stood out against the Greek side, scoring a hat-trick in an encouraging sign that the 2024 player of the year is returning to his best.

The midfielder was dropped by England for last summer’s World Cup after two indifferent seasons with City and also served a domestic suspension earlier in the season after being sent off in the Manchester derby.

Foden said: “Obviously I had the unfortunate red card against Man United but I think the break did me good. I came back really fresh and sharp.

“I’ve been involved in a lot of goals lately and I’ve been really happy with my own performance. Hopefully I can get back to that level. I think I’m starting to get back there now. Hopefully I keep growing and getting better.”

Asked about his England prospects, he said: “It is one of those things. Football is full of ups and downs and it’s one of those things you can’t control.

“You just have to keep trying your best on the field and keep putting in performances. Hopefully, one day, the call-up might come back.”

Asked if he had heard from England manager Thomas Tuchel lately, he said: “I haven’t really spoken to him. There’s not much to say on that.”

Foden has still been on the bench for City’s last two Premier League games despite his recent improvement.

Maresca said: “We are in all competitions and we have 20 senior players – all of them very good – so there’s competition between them.

“We have so many games and many players. It’s not a short run, it’s not a sprint. It’s a marathon.

“It’s very important, for sure, in this moment to win games but it’s also very, very important to arrive in February, March, April, when things are going to be more exciting, having all of them available and fit.”

#1007. Germany news: Emergency at Leipzig airport sparked by novice driver

Two men breached a fence at the Leipzig/Halle airport while practicing for a driving test. Meanwhile, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced an industrial AI partnership with Nvidia. DW has more.

This blog is now closed. Below is a roundup of the stories from and about Germany on Monday, October 19, 2026.

Berlin's Left Party, the Greens and the Social Democrats are set to move ahead on talks to form the next coalition government in the capital city.

The SPD's state leadership approved the motion with a wide majority in an online session, and the Greens voted overwhelmingly in favor of talks at a small party convention.

The Left Party has not scheduled a conference until October 31 because members of the party may be away because of school holidays.

The Left Party is hoping to have Elif Eralp lead the state government.

The coalition talks are set to open after weeks of tense negotiations and a dispute over alleged antisemitism within the ranks of the Left Party.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang unveiled a new artificial intelligence (AI) cooperation at a glitzy investment summit in Berlin on Monday evening.

"Germany is open for business," said Merz at the Invest in Germany event, adding that the combination of German engineering and cutting-edge AI technology would help strengthen the country's economy in the long term.

"Germany is open for investment and Germany is ready to grow at a faster pace," the chancellor continued, before joking: "If I were Jensen Huang, I would put on my leather jacket, take a flight to Berlin, meet the German Chancellor, and tell him, 'I'm ready to invest.'"

The partnership with Nvidia is intended to speed up the digital transformation of German industry and secure the country's technological sovereignty.

According to the company, Nvidia invested nearly $1 billion in Germany last year and holds stakes in numerous start-ups and established companies.

But Europe's largest economy has nevertheless struggled to attract foreign investment after years of weak growth, with high energy prices and labor costs continuing to deter businesses.

German officials were hoping that Monday's summit, which was attended by more than 200 domestic and international investment executives, would showcase Germany as an attractive investment destination, highlighting its sound public finances, status as the only G7 country with a triple-A credit rating, its universities, skilled workforce and tariff-free trade within the EU single market.

Further behind-closed-door talks are set to take place on Tuesday.

Do you remember those arrests in Germany last week, connected to an arson attempt at a Starlink control center in Poland?

The government in Warsaw called it a hybrid attack and accused Russia of recruiting organized crime elements for the alleged crime.

It's much too early to say for sure, but Bulgaria has now issued a pair of European arrest warrants against German citizens in a case that seems rather reminiscent in several regards.

The two 19-year-olds are accused of driving in from Serbia claiming to be tourists, setting fire to a series of antennae south of Sofia, and leaving the country again within a matter of hours.

Hermann Höllenreiner, a Sinti German raised in Bavaria who survived the Nazis' Auschwitz concentration camp as a child, has died aged 92.

Munich's Hanser Verlag publisher and the International Auschwitz Committee said that he had passed away last Friday, October 16, in Mettenheim in Bavaria, surrounded by his family.

Höllenreiner, known as "Mano" to his large Bavarian Sinti family, spent time at the Auschwitz-Birkenau, Ravensbrück and Sachsenhausen camps as a child.

"Only later in his life did he start to tell his story and became a major witness of the era, who hauntingly reported on the horrors of Auschwitz, the perpetrators and the victims, and above all of the still-persistnent discrimination of Sinti and Roma in Europe," Christioph Heubner, executive vice president of the International Auschwitz Committee, said.

"Mano Höllenreiner's biography and tales of suffering were enough for more than one life. What he saw with his own eyes as a child in Auschwitz and what was done to him — for many decades he didn't know how to speak out about it," Heubner said, thanking Höllenreiner for his "courage and humanity" in ultimately telling his story.

Höllenriener managed to flee one of the so-called "death marches" fleeing extermination camps in as Allied armies approached.

Author Anja Tuckermann told his story in a book whose title roughly translates as: "Mano. The boy who didn't know where he was."

He was initially found on a roadside and rescued by liberated French prisoners, who took him home with them. In 1946, he was reunited with surviving relatives in Germany.

Two men have admitted to breaking through a fence at Leipzig/Halle airport while one of them was practicing for a driving test, an incident that triggered a major security operation, police said on Monday.

The two, aged 20 and 32, handed themselves in to the police on Sunday evening, following the incident. The broken fence was first discovered by airport staff late on Saturday.

Police said the 20-year-old had been at the wheel despite not having a valid license.

An investigation was opened into the learner driver for fleeing the scene after breaking through the fence.

The mass-circulation Bild newspaper reported that the car involved, of which fragments were found at the site, was an Audi.

The airport was the site of a security scare in August, when an explosives-laden drone was found there near Ukrainian cargo planes.

German officials accused Russia of having planned an attack, something Moscow denied.

Germany's Rheinmetall defense group on Monday announced that it had acquired Romania's Mangalia shipyard at auction in partnership with Swiss shipping giant MSC.

Rheinmetall said it had paid approximately €138 million ($154 million) for the facility.   Acquisition is expected to be finalized within a few weeks.   Rheinmetall and MSC plan to develop the Black Sea shipyard near Constanța into a dual-use site for civilian and military shipbuilding for both domestic and international markets.

Rheinmetall says its Naval Systems division will use the facility to build four vessels commissioned by the Romanian government, including two 96-meter (305 foot) offshore patrol vessels and two 43-meter diving support vessels.   The company also intends to modernize the shipyard's infrastructure and expand its capacity.

"In doing so," said the company, ​"Rheinmetall ⁠is creating a scalable foundation for future ⁠projects in ​southeastern Europe and strengthens its position in a strategically important market."

The Foreign Ministry has summoned Iran's ambassador after two men were convicted of preparing attacks on Jewish figures and pro-Israel targets in Germany at the behest of Tehran.

"We vehemently condemn Iran's activities. We will not allow Iran to threaten our liberal society," the ministry wrote on X.

"We do not tolerate attacks on Jewish life and those who defend it anywhere, and particularly not in Germany," it wrote.

A Hamburg court on Thursday sentenced a 54-year-old man and a 43-year old man respectively to 8 1/2 and 4 1/2 years in prison for having spied on the president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, Josef Schuster, and Volker Beck, the president of the German-Israeli Society (DIG).

In the court's opinion, their actions were carried out in preparation for terrorist attacks, including the planned murders of  Schuster and Beck.

The court said the 54-year-old, who was said to have also done the groundwork for an arson attack on a kosher food store in Berlin, received his orders directly from officers in the Quds Force.

The Quds Force is the branch of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) that is in charge of extraterritorial operations.

German industrial businesses employed some 496,000 fewer people at the end of 2025 compared to the start of 2019, according to a survey conducted by the Ifo Institute economic think tank.

Worst-hit has been the automotive industry, a key sector of the German economy, where 123,500 jobs were cut both at carmakers and suppliers, a decline of 13%.

But the metals sector also saw a marked decline in the number of jobs available, dropping 115,600 workers in the period, while the machinery sector bled 64,500 positions.

At the same time, more than 2.2 million additional jobs were created in the service sector, according to Ifo.

It said 391,000 new jobs had been established in the health sector and another 357,000 in social services, including care homes.

Joachim Ragnitz, managing director at Ifo Dresden, said the figures showed an "accelerated structural shift" in Germany.

"Ironically, the very sectors that have sustained our prosperity up to now are shrinking," he said.

"The new jobs are for the most part not being created where Germany is especially productive and innovative. That may slow down our growth potential in the future."

A German woman has died in a climbing accident in the Italian Alps, mountain rescuers said on Monday.

The 32-year-old woman, who was an experienced mountaineer, fell more than 50 meters (164 feet) to her death while on the Cengia dei Camosci, a difficult route on the 2,323-meter Grande Nabois mountain near the Slovenian border.

The rescue service said the accident was caused when a climbing hold gave way under the woman, who was accompanied by an Austrian fellow climber at the time.

Investigations are underway to clarify the exact circumstances of her death.

Carmaker Volkswagen intends to freeze the salaries of some 660,000 employees worldwide until 2030 as the company, along with the entire car industry, faces a range of challenges that have impacted its profits.

Trade union IG Metall confirmed earlier media reports of the plans, citing information given to employees by the works council.

The works council described the plans as unrealistic and said there would be considerable resistance to them.

If the company does implement them, employees could lose an estimated 10% of their purchasing power by the end of the decade.

The news comes after VW decided in September to cut 50,000 jobs worldwide in the coming years in addition to the reduction of 50,000 positions that had already been agreed.

Four plants in Germany are also at risk of being closed between 2031 and 2034.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Less than a third of leadership positions in Germany are held by women, a lower level than the EU average, statistics released on Monday showed.

According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), citing figures from the EU statistics authority Eurostat, women held just 30.3% of leadership positions in Germany, compared with 35.9% in the whole of the EU.

Only Cyprus, Italy and the Netherlands have lower rates than Germany in the bloc, while Sweden has the highest, at 44.4%, followed by Latvia, Estonia and Poland.

"The low proportion of women in leadership positions in Germany is particularly striking, as almost as many women as men are employed here," Destatis said, comparing the situation with Italy, which has almost the same level of female leadership but a much lower rate of female employment overall.

Destatis defines leadership positions as those involving the management of small companies, the management of large companies or departments within them and high administrative posts.

A two-day conference entitled "Invest in Germany Summit" is to begin on Monday evening in Berlin as the government seeks to shore up public-sector spending with private money.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz will deliver the opening speech at the conference, which will be attended by an expected 200 representatives from large German and international companies.

The CEO of the US chip manufacturer Nvidia, Jensen Huang, is to be one of the key guests at the conference.

The German government is looking to cooperate strongly with the company, whose products are central to the boom in artificial intelligence, in a bid to help Germany catch up in the sector.

The German Economic Institute (IW) has, however, warned against any too high expectations from the summit, saying that high costs for labor, energy and bureaucracy in Germany were a deterrent to investment in the country.

"It would be naive to believe that the summit will change that in the short term. Companies don't choose Germany because of a promotional event. What matters is whether they can make money here," IW director Michael Hüther told the DPA news agency.

He said it would be more effective if the government were to swiftly implement its reform agenda.

A study by Allianz Research has shown that investment in Germany fell by 6.4% between 2019 and 2025, while it grew by 6.7% in the rest of the eurozone and a whole 20.2% in the US.

The DW newsroom in Bonn bids guten Tag to all its faithful readers at the start of a new week!

Today, we will be looking at a conference in Berlin that will seek to attract private investment in Germany to help make the country fit for the future, with the field of artificial intelligence a key focus.

New statistics are also to be released on Monday on women in leadership and government positions in Germany and the EU in 2025.

And the Leipzig/Halle airport has resumed normal operations after a security incident involving a breached fence triggered a large-scale police operation.

This occurred just weeks after an explosives-laden drone that German officials believe was intended to carry out an attack on behalf of Russia was found at the airport.

Teenage sensation Freddy Adu was tipped for superstardom and got a trial at Manchester United - but it didn't work out

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Big things were once expected for American playmaker Freddy Adu, who to this day remains perplexed as to why he never got what could have been a career-changing move to England.

Aged just 17 and already a long-established regular in MLS with DC United, Adu was taken on trial at Manchester United in November 2006, and was persistently linked with a move to Old Trafford.

But the move never came about, with Adu briefly moving to Real Salt Lake before heading to Benfica in a $2m.

That turned out to be the start of year upon year of being a squad player at over a dozen clubs for Adu, who told FourFourTwo: "Honestly, I don’t know why the [Manchester United] move didn't happen. I was young and I had my agent bringing me all these offers.

"Benfica just seemed like the best jump for me at the time, the place where I’d have the best chance of playing and developing.

"It didn’t turn out to be that way. My agent thought Benfica was a good idea, and the people around me, my advisors. Everybody did think that Benfica was best for me.

"For me, personally, Portugal’s a great league, but at that time in America, we didn’t know much about the Portuguese league.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"We knew more about the English league, the Spanish, the Italian, the German, so I wanted to go to one of those. That was always my dream.

"But with the options that were presented, my agent, the adults in the room, thought Benfica was a good jumping-off point.

"Everybody wants to end up playing for one of the bigger clubs in the world, so that was in the back of my mind, but once I got to Benfica, I realised how big Benfica were and how awesome the atmosphere was.

"The thing that soured me on Benfica was going through three different coaches in my first year there, and how it was just so up and down everything.

"A new coach comes in, they have their own ideas, they have their own guys that they want to play. Then another coach comes in, he has his own guy...it was just all over the place.

"It was my first season in Europe, and it was quite immediately unsettling. Everything started going sideways and downwards after that."

Steven Chicken has been working as a football writer since 2009, taking in stints with Football365 and the Huddersfield Examiner. #1005. HENRY WINTER: Declan Rice is a winner, Arsenal's most important player - and could use Ballon d'Or disappointment to reach another level

Arsenal midfielder Declan Rice is a player Mikel Arteta dare not substitute, and was the difference at Anfield once more in an ever-impressive run, writes Henry Winter

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In what was inevitably a hugely competitive Ballon d’Or in a World Cup year, some exceptional talents were always going to miss out on votes.

Arsenal won the most demanding title in the world, the Premier League, and fought their way to the Champions League final. They boasted eight players who reached the semi-finals of the World Cup, and three Spaniards who won it, yet Arsenal’s highest-ranked player in the Ballon d’Or was only 15th - Declan Rice. Frustration at that lack of recognition may provide further fuel driving them through this season.

As one of the Ballon d’Or judges, I was determined to cast a vote for Rice, even if it meant only one point in placing him 10th. The excellence of Rice’s season deserved acknowledgement. He should have been named Footballer of the Year by the writers, and he certainly got my vote, but our industry plumped for Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes, who’s grabbing headlines for different reasons now.

I backed Rice because he’s a winner. The three criteria that the Ballon d’Or organisers, France Football, tell us to adhere to are essentially individual performance, collective performance (i.e. trophies) and role model qualities. (It’s why Harry Kane won overall).

Rice delivered on all counts, and he continues this season, registering five assists already from midfield, targeting further glory with Arsenal defending their title, and playing the game the right way. Rice doesn’t dive. He’d get in any midfield, barring possibly Paris Saint-Germain’s.

The best compliment that can be paid to Arsenal’s box-to-box destroyer and assist-maker is that he looks increasingly the natural midfield heir to Patrick Vieira, captain of the club’s greatest team, the Invincibles of 2003/04. In Sunday’s demanding game at Anfield with the stakes high, and the pressure even higher, Rice again rose to the occasion. He put in a pacey, well-timed overlap and cross for Kai Havertz’s goal, and then provided constant, mobile resistance when Liverpool threatened.

He’s a no.6, increasingly a no.8, who has responded to Mikel Arteta’s pre-season encouragement to attack more. He combines elite technique and temperament. He showed his quick feet to whisk the ball around Florian Wirtz, used his right foot to create Havertz’s goal, and then his left foot to ping a pass down the line to Havertz. He twice closed down Bradley Barcola. He toyed with Ronald Araujo before crossing to Noni Madueke.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

He is now, unquestionably, Arsenal’s most important player, especially with Bukayo Saka struggling for sustained fitness. He’s surely the eventual successor to Martin Odegaard as captain. The club are currently looking to tie Rice, 27, down to the most significant contract of his career, taking him through his peak years.

He’s so important that Arteta dare not take him off. Rice completed 90 minutes in the win against Liverpool, in the draw against Bayern Munich when he scored at the Allianz, in the victory at Napoli, the home win over Leeds United and away win at Nottingham Forest. He played all but five minutes of the triumph at Aston Villa.

That also stirs concern around the vexed issue of over-playing. Rice endured neural pain in his hamstring in the second half of last season. The England international did have a three-week rest when withdrawing from consideration for the last international break. Thomas Tuchel will doubtless want his most powerful midfielder returning for the forthcoming Nations League games against Croatia at Wembley and away to Spain at the Metropolitano in Madrid.

Only a mathematical meltdown – an 8-0 loss to Croatia - would deny England qualification to the Nations League quarter-finals. England will want to overhaul Spain, and finish top of Group A3, ensuring they play a runner-up in March (the semi-finals and final are June 9-13), so Tuchel is likely to go strong. There will inevitably be some club managers hoping their players are rested.

That is a conversation for Tuchel and Arteta to have. Rice always wants to represent England, adding to his 80 caps. He’s currently joint 22nd in the all-time appearance list with Gary Lineker, and would climb into the top 20, past Rio Ferdinand and alongside Raheem Sterling, if he features against Croatia and Spain.

He has so much to offer club and country.

Henry Winter is one of football's most popular and respected writers. Previously the Chief Football Writer for The Times and a Football Correspondent for The Daily Telegraph, his work now primarily features on his Substack. He has also lauched his own podcast 'The Winter View'

#1004. Barcelona sweep aside Aston Villa as Unai Emery endures another miserable Nou Camp night

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Barcelona 3-0 Aston Villa: Raphinha scored twice to secure a comfortable win for the hosts

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Unai Emery endured another difficult visit to the Nou Camp as his Aston Villa side were defeated 3-0 by Barcelona in the Champions League.

An early goal from Lamine Yamal alongside two second-half strikes from Raphinha – who has now scored 19 goals in 13 appearances this campaign – ensured a disappointing 55th birthday for the Spanish manager.

Emery has now suffered defeat in 15 of his 16 trips to face Barcelona, a dismal record headlined by the infamous 6-1 loss with Paris Saint-Germain nine years ago following a 4-0 first-leg advantage.

Watched by super fan Prince William, this fixture represented a major milestone in Villa’s development across the four years of Emery’s reign.

While the loss brought an end to their flawless start in the league phase, the visitors might have altered the outcome had they converted a series of promising first-half opportunities.

Nevertheless, with winnable fixtures remaining, Villa retain strong prospects of securing a place in the top eight.

Against a prolific Barcelona side, Villa’s defensive lapse in the opening minutes proved costly.

Trying to play out from a seventh-minute goal-kick, Joao Gomes mistakenly delivered a pass straight to Yamal, who curled a finish into the corner from 12 yards out.

Despite the poor start, Villa almost restored parity immediately through consecutive corners.

Matty Cash saw his low strike deflected wide at the back post before Gomes had a close-range effort thwarted by a fine block from Joao Cancelo.

Settling into the contest, Villa exposed Barcelona’s high defensive line. They should have levelled in the 19th minute when Nicolas Jackson burst down the right flank to set up Johan Manzambi, who shot wide.

Jackson then raced through once more, only for rushing goalkeeper Joan Garcia to intervene with a crucial foot-tackle.

At the other end, Zion Suzuki briefly put Villa in jeopardy playing from the back, though he quickly redeemed himself by saving an attempt from Anthony Gordon.

Manzambi then threatened again, driving into the penalty area only to see his effort halted by Garcia.

Those missed chances proved decisive when Barcelona doubled their advantage in the 52nd minute. Fermin Lopez picked out Raphinha on the edge of the area, and his shot deflected off Pau Torres’ heel into the net.

Twelve minutes later, the hosts added a third as Cancelo evaded John McGinn to cross for Raphinha, who scored comfortably from six yards.

Villa attempted to respond, with Leon Goretzka sending a glancing header against the post.

However, Barcelona remained dominant late on. Another misplaced pass from Suzuki exposed Boubacar Kamara, though the Japanese international denied Fermin’s follow-up shot, before Yamal – now the highest-scoring teenager in Champions League history – narrowly missed with two further efforts.

#1002. McIlroy gives view on claims LIV Golf wanted to 'destroy' DP World Tour

Rory McIlroy hopes men's golf can now have a reset after LIV Golf's attempts to "destroy" the DP World Tour; McIlroy was speaking ahead of the Abu Dhabi Albar Championship, live on Sky Sports Golf from Thursday

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Rory McIlroy has claimed LIV Golf officials were saying they 'wanted to destroy the European Tour' during their visit to The Masters this year.

McIlroy successfully defended his Green Jacket at Augusta National in April, less than three weeks before Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) confirmed it would end funding for LIV Golf at the end of the season.

LIV Golf has since acquired new investment as they look to relaunch in 2027, despite many high-profile players - including Jon Rahm, Tyrrell Hatton and Sergio Garcia - confirming they wouldn't re-sign with the league and would return to the DP World Tour.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

DP World Tour chief executive Guy Kinnings told The Scotsman last week that LIV Golf looked to 'destroy' the European circuit, having targeted DP World Tour events and sponsors, with McIlroy backing those suggestions and questioning the rival circuit.

"I agree with everything that Guy [Kinnings] said," McIlroy admitted ahead of the Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship, live on Sky Sports. "They [LIV Golf] took players; they took sponsors; they turned professional golf into an arms race.

"They were going around Augusta saying they wanted to destroy The European Tour (DP World Tour). Yeah, I agree with everything. I think people that don't agree are probably very short-sighted.

"There was some of the money that they used the right way, created the International Series on the Asian Tour, great for a couple years, but where did that leave the Asian Tour? They left them high and dry.

"Asian Tour came back into the fold, did a partnership with the PGA Tour and the European Tour - again, this was always going to be the case.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"It was always going to be good for a few years until something like this happened, or they realised they weren't going to get any return on investment, or they were going to leave the golf space and go invest in something else and invest in something that would actually make them money.

"I think for long-term sustainability for men's professional golf, I think we are in a much better spot."

Sky Sports reached out to LIV Golf for comment over Kinnings' claims, since reiterated by McIlroy.

Rahm said on Tuesday he left LIV Golf because he "wasn't willing to follow" the path that the new iteration of the circuit was taking, with McIlroy hoping that the men's game can now stabilise after a turbulent few years.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"We'll look back on it as a very strange time," McIlroy added. "It gave players a lot of leverage over the tours and I don't necessarily think that's a good thing for the overall health of the professional game.

"They created a false economy within men's professional golf, and I think that there is going to be a bit of a reset here - just for things to be a little bit more sustainable. There's not as much of an arms race as there was maybe a couple of years ago.

"Some players will argue that that's not good for players, but I think that's very short-term thinking. If you want sustainable tours, and we want these tours around in 50 years' time, there has to be sustainable business practises in place to make sure they are around in 50 years' time."

Fortress Anfield is no more. Arsenal proved Liverpool have lost their fear factor.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Liverpool certainly didn’t lack effort or endeavour in their 1-0 defeat to Arsenal at Anfield, and were denied a clear penalty for Jurrien Timber’s shirt pull on Alexander Isak in the first half, but another home defeat underlines where Andoni Iraola’s side must improve.

For the Reds’ new Spanish boss, the 90 minutes against Mikel Arteta’s defensively-excellent side showed exactly where Liverpool are at in their development.

The headline stat of zero Opta-defined shots on target for the home side for the first time since records began in 2003 tells the story in more way than one.

Liverpool’s attack struggled against Arteta’s team that thrives defensively, especially when going a goal ahead early in the game.

It was that early part of the game that Iraola chose to focus on post-match, saying: “Overall, I think we have to blame especially the start of the game and until we conceded the goal. I think the start hasn't been at the level of the game.”

Liverpool recovered well, but breaking down the champions who are more than happy to sit on a 1-0 lead and defend like a prime Tony Pulis or Sam Allardyce-drilled side is a thankless task.

It gets results, even more so when their tactic of delaying any momentum being built by the opposition is so easily bought by the referee.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

No wonder Virgil van Dijk admitted post-match that he shared Liverpool fans’ frustration at the fouls being awarded every time a Liverpool player went near a man in an Arsenal shirt.

“I got a card towards the end, so I probably shared it as well," the Dutchman said.

But for all the frustration at Arsenal’s antics and the referee’s inability to see through it, Liverpool’s front three of Isak, Cody Gakpo and Bradley Barcola simply have to offer more if they are to win games like these.

Barcola doesn’t look adjusted to this level of fixture in the Premier League yet. The Frenchman certainly puts in the work off the ball and contests plenty of duels (losing 12 of the 18 he contested), but going forward more will be needed from the £123 million signing.

The reality is that this front three of Isak, Gakpo and Barcola - signed for a combined sum just shy of £300m - are currently a far-cry from the Firmino, Salah, Mane trio that combined physical presence with quality output. Opposition defences certainly don't fear this new-look attack the way they did previously.

Florian Wirtz, in the No. 10 role behind the front three, was a busy presence, frequently the available option to play out and find pockets of space, and never shying away from the difficult task of playing in that area of the pitch against this Arsenal side. Again, though, he was signed to be the player to unlock such defences.

Liverpool did have 17 attempts on goal and 48 touches inside Arsenal’s box, but the final pass or finish wasn’t there.

And while Arsenal aren’t an easy team to open up, finding ways to do so is what’s required if you are to compete at the top and win the big games. Sunday afternoon marked Arsenal’s first win at Anfield in 14 years.

Iraola knows where his side must improve, having scored the fewest goals of the teams in the top seven of the table after nine games played, saying: “I think we've had a lot of situations inside the box – not even around the box, inside the box – that definitely we haven't finished properly.”

When Liverpool are next at Anfield it’s the visit of Manchester United after the international break, by which point the Reds will have won one home league game in almost seven months. Of course, that spans the end of Arne Slot’s tenure, the summer, and two international breaks, but one win from five home league matches for Iraola is far from ideal.

Much is made of ‘Fortress Anfield’ but for the past two seasons that has been far from the case. Last season, the Reds failed to win nine of their 19 home league games. Failing to win 47% of your home games isn’t going to get you anywhere near the title. This season, albeit five games in, it’s 20%. Teams no longer fear coming to Anfield.

Last year, Man United registered their first win at Anfield since 2016. Forest, who recorded consecutive wins at Anfield for the first time since the 1960s, are now three unbeaten at Anfield. It’s a similar story for Manchester City, winning their last two visits after going 23 years without doing so, with fans in attendance.

It’s not just the big clubs who have come away from Anfield unscathed; Fulham, Sunderland, Leeds, Burnley and Brentford in the last year have all collected points.

And therein lies the issue, if Liverpool can’t find ways to break down teams that play defensively at Anfield, they will struggle to compete for the title. In their five home games this season they’ve scored just four goals - their lowest since 2012.

Iraola, of course, knows this, and he has also acknowledged the need to get the crowd onside and how important it is to start games well in order to do so.

It’s clear where Liverpool need to improve, so the Kop can chant ‘Attack, Attack, Attack’ again.

Matt Ladson is the co-founder and editor of This Is Anfield, the independent Liverpool news and comment website, and covers all areas of the Reds for FourFourTwo – including transfer analysis, interviews, title wins and European trophies. As well as writing about Liverpool for FourFourTwo he also contributes to other titles including Yahoo and Bleacher Report. He is a lifelong fan of the Reds.

#1000. Bulgaria seeks suspects in Germany after Starlink sabotage

A Bulgarian court has issued arrest warrants for two young German nationals suspected of setting fire to Starlink antennas. The case is reminiscent of another in Poland, which Warsaw says was orchestrated by Russia.

Bulgaria on Monday issued European arrest warrants against two 19-year-old German nationals, saying it suspected their involvement in the sabotage of a series of Starlink antennas near the capital Sofia.

"The evidence gathered makes it possible to conclude that there are reasonable grounds to suspect the involvement of the two defendants," the court in Sofia rules, granting a request from prosecutors.

Ukraine's military uses Starlink's military-grade satellite internet service Starshield for battlefield communications amid Russia's invasion.

Bulgaria does not directly border Ukraine, but it is on the Black Sea, one of the flashpoints of the conflict. A similar case in Poland, which does directly border Ukraine, led to a total of four arrests last week, also in Germany.

The two teenage suspects are accused of deliberately setting fire to the antennas on the evening of October 9.

Of 18 in a mountainous region south of Sofia, three were destroyed entirely, two were partially burned and three more were damaged, according to prosecutors.

Prosecutors say the suspects entered from Serbia in a car with German license plates, claiming to be tourists, staying just a few hours around the time of the alleged crime.

Plamen Tonchev, the head of Bulgaria's domestic intelligence agency DANS, said he was working on the assumption that it was deliberate sabotage and said other such acts could not be ruled out in future.

News of the arrests follow just a week after a total of four people were arrested in Germany, accused of sabotaging a Starlink satellite communications station in central Poland in late September.

German police detained three resident men and a woman, two of them Turkish nationals, early last week.

Polish officials said they believed that Russia was behind the sabotage attempt, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk calling it an act of "hybrid warfare."

The domestic intelligence agency also claimed that Russia had cooperated with organized crime elements in Germany on the alleged operation.

Meanwhile, in the Baltic, Lithuania's prime minister on Sunday said that Russia was likely behind an attempted arson attack on a company hosting communication hardware for Starlink satellites.

#996. Brutal, revolutionary empire builder: Genghis Khan's legacy

Berlin is host to a major exhibition on the founder of the Mongol Empire and his successors. Here's how Genghis Khan disrupted the course of history.

Genghis Khan is one of history's most radical figures. A blood-thirsty invader whose conquests caused the deaths of an estimated 40 million people, he was also a visionary political thinker who established the largest contiguous land empire in history.

The founder of the Mongolian Empire died in 1227. Ahead of the 800th anniversary of his death, Berlin's James-Simon-Galerie explores his legacy and the "Mongol Century" (1250–1350) in the exhibition "Genghis Khan and the World of the Mongols."

The ruler remains "incredibly relevant" to this day, says Matthias Wemhoff, the director of the exhibition project.

"What the era of Genghis Khan — the 'Mongol century,' if you will — vividly demonstrates is how quickly established structures can collapse, how rapidly vast empires can vanish from the map and how swiftly the entire landscape can be utterly transformed," the archaeologist tells DW.

The charismatic leader's unprecedented impact on the world also evokes present-day disruptive individuals who are triggering sudden, unpredictable societal shifts, says Wemhoff: "There's always been this question: Are world politics shaped by individuals or rather by groups and sociological processes?"

In this case, the answer is clear, says the museum director, who also co-wrote a 2026 book on the nomadic leader.

"If Genghis Khan hadn't existed, the course of world history would truly have been entirely different — so much of it is inextricably linked to his person," Wemhoff says.

Genghis Khan was born as Temujin around the year 1162. His father, a Mongol chieftain called Yesugei, died when he was still a child. His family was abandoned by its tribe. To secure his familial position, Temujin killed his older half-brother, Bekter, when he was still a young teenager.

Thanks to his charismatic personality, he built alliances and found followers who helped him become the sole ruler on the Mongolian steppe. He formally adopted the title of Genghis Khan in 1206.

At its peak, the Mongol Empire covered approximately 24 million square kilometers (about 9.3 million square miles), stretching from China and Korea to parts of Eastern Europe and the Middle East, and accounting for over 16% of the Earth's total land area.

Wemhoff lists various innovations under his rule: For one, Genghis Khan transformed warfare. Commanders were promoted for skill, discipline and loyalty rather than based on aristocratic rank or tribal loyalties. Soldiers were organized into decimal units of 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000.

Despite being illiterate by modern standards, he also pushed for the introduction of the first written script for the Mongolian language, which allowed to build a state bureaucracy, track population and tax registers, record decrees, issue legal decisions and handle diplomacy.

A set of laws were established that replaced fragmented tribal customs with a unified legal system.

Trade was simplified through his adoption of a paper currency.

A policy of religious freedom was also established across the Mongol Empire, allowing all individuals to practice their chosen faith without state coercion.

Before the Mongol Empire, the Silk Road was fragmented by local conflicts and heavy taxes. Mongol rule placed the entire route under a single authority, making long-distance travel vastly safer.

The Mongol Empire is known as a period of relative political stability, economic growth and cultural exchange, an era historians call the "Pax Mongolica."

But "it all came with incredible levels of cruelty. The millions of people who fell victim to the Mongols — the mass executions, the abuse of women — this happened on a scale previously unheard of," notes Wemhoff.

The exhibition opens with a raid that happened after Genghis Khan's death, but took place just 260 kilometers (around 160 miles) away from Berlin: the 1241 Battle of Legnica, in Silesia, Poland.

It embodies the brutality and intensity of the Mongols' methods.

There came the "highly mobile, agile Mongols on small horses — lightly armored in lamellar gear, wearing helmets that left the face exposed, and wielding bows capable of firing 20 or more arrows in a single minute," points out Wemhoff.

European knights, heavily armored and mounted on large, massive warhorses, didn't stand a chance against their enemies.

"When a hail of arrows rained down on them, the horses eventually went down, and the knights ended up lying on the ground, stuck on their back, much like a June bug," he adds. "The two styles of combat were simply mismatched."

The Mongols' western campaigns shifted historic power centers in a way that still impacts world politics today.

For example, after the Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus', which was the first East Slavic state, its thriving capital Kyiv was reduced to a depopulated ruin. Moscow became a key regional power, partly because it chose to cooperate with the Mongols rather than pursue resistance.

"In our Western European collective memory, the Mongol invasion plays hardly any role. It's something of an anecdote," says Wemhoff, noting that the era of Genghis Khan and his immediate successors is barely mentioned in standard Western European school curricula.

Germans are mainly familiar with the name of the empire's founder through the 1979 Euro-disco pop band Dschingis Khan, which represented West Germany at the Eurovision Song Contest with a campy song of the same name that reduced complex history to extreme tropes.

But in eastern Europe, the Mongol invasions "changed everything fundamentally," says Wemhoff. "And so fundamentally that we still feel the consequences of it today."

The exhibition "Genghis Khan and the World of the Mongols" runs from October 21, 2026, to April 18, 2027.

#994. Man United latest: Michael Carrick’s job saved by brilliant Champions League comeback against Roma

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Man United 3-2 Roma: United end nine-game winless streak in remarkable fashion by battling back from 2-0 down to snatch priceless victory

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Michael Carrick saw his job saved in the most remarkable way as Manchester United fought back from 2-0 down against Roma in the Champions League to snatch the unlikeliest of 3-2 wins at Old Trafford.

Carrick, who had seen United go winless in nine games for the first time in 40 years, was desperate for a change of fortunes to save his skin but his time at Old Trafford appeared to be coming to an end as the hopeless Red Devils were 2-0 down inside 20 minutes as part of a diabolical first-half display.

But they were a different team in the second half and were given a lifeline when Bruno Fernandes scored a re-taken penalty – with a Roma player encroaching into the area during the initial miss – after Matheus Cunha was fouled.

Cunha then became the hero when he capitalised on a Roma error seven minutes from time to equalise before firing a winning goal in style shortly after, although he was booked for his celebration and then sent off injury time after an clumsy lunging tackle earned a deserved second yellow.

There was huge relief for Carrick who will head into a crunch clash with Aston Villa on Sunday with at least a little bit of confidence restored as he looks to come back from the brink. Follow all the reaction from Man United’s remarkable comeback win over Roma in our live blog below:

Bruno Fernandes denied that Manchester United’s remarkable comeback win against Roma saved Michael Carrick from the sack but admitted the manager was right to drop him for criticising his tactics last month.

He said: “The manager took a decision of making myself be on the bench because I wasn’t performing, and that’s fair.

“Everyone felt that was a punishment for the words that I had said. And if it was, it was right. The manager is the one that makes the decisions. I have to accept them. I have to go forward with that.

“It doesn’t change the belief I have on the manager and on the staff and and every player that is in this club, and it doesn’t change my aim to win every f***ing game that I have ahead of me.”

Manchester United have snapped their nine-game winless streak. It was the worst run the club had seen since 1984. Their results since victory over Sabah in September were:

But after last night’s turnaround, United are back in the win column.

Michael Carrick may still need a greater comeback than this if he is to keep his job. But even if it does prove his last Champions League night at Old Trafford, at least he was given a glimpse of the Manchester United he remembers and which, increasingly, had seemed consigned to the past.

There was an extraordinary fightback, a victory plucked from the jaws of defeat. The crowd who had reacted to the award of a penalty by calling for the Glazer family to go ended up galvanised and roused, cheering a team who had been an absolute embarrassment for 45 minutes to a victory few saw coming,

Carrick had said he knew it sounded crazy when he said he was looking forward to this game. By half-time, his optimism appeared delusional. But now and again, even when they are at their lowest ebb for decades, United can justify the faith.

"We needed a bit of a kick,” he said on Amazon Prime Video. “We were a bit reactionary. When we lost the ball, we weren't reacting as quickly as we could have and the boss really drilled it into us that we need to be more active and take the game ourselves.

"We know what we're capable of. We know we're a dangerous team and we know we can change a game whenever, it's just it all coming together at the right time. It has tonight and hopefully we carry it on for the rest of the season."

The producers on Amazon Prime Video might have had a bit of a scare to see Bruno Fernandes drop an F-bomb live on air, but Wayne Rooney was delighted to see that passion overflowing from the Man United captain.

“Bruno Fernandes has shown a bit of passion in defending himself on what he thought was right, but more importantly we have seen that passion and fight on the pitch because the first half was terrible,” he said. “The first half had none of what we saw in the second half.

“No passion, no tackling, no getting to the ball, no aggression, and the complete opposite of the second half.

“And when that happens in the second half, you see the crowd get behind the team and you felt like they were going to win the game.”

Manchester United are back in the win column - but Michael Carrick isn’t out of hot water yet.

Tonight’s win should give him until at least the international break. Now focus turns to the Premier League, where his side are hovering above the relegation zone on goal difference.

#993. US social sciences face existential crisis after NSF cuts

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Dan Garisto is a freelance reporter in Syracuse, New York.

The future of US archaeology is cloudy after the collapse of the main federal funding source for social sciences.Credit: Derek Davis/Portland Press Herald/Getty

After a long day excavating a prehistoric campsite in eastern Wyoming, Todd Surovell would lie down in a tent and imagine a former era. “I would think about what it would sound like to hear a herd of mammoths walk by, to put yourself in that world,” he says. “How would you behave? What would your social network look like?”

Now, Surovell, a palaeoanthropologist at the University of Wyoming in Laramie, lies awake for a different reason. The funding source that has enabled much of his research so far, and that of generations of US archaeologists, economists and other social scientists, is being dismantled.

NSF plans cuts to core science programmes to fund White House initiative

NSF plans cuts to core science programmes to fund White House initiative

The US National Science Foundation (NSF) has long provided the bulk of US research funding for the social sciences. “For a lot of economists, it’s really the NSF or nothing,” says Michael Woodford, an economist at Columbia University in New York City, who won a share of the 2026 Nobel prize in economic science for his contributions to fiscal-stability theories.

But that support has plummeted over the past two years. In the 2026 fiscal year, which ended on 30 September, the agency funded fewer than 100 new social-science grants, compared with a historical average of roughly 850 per year, according to data from Grant Witness, a non-profit organization tracking US research funding, and from the NSF.

The agency awarded no new grants at all in dozens of programme areas, including archaeology and economics — although it proudly announced in October that the number of Nobel-winning economists who have had NSF support now stands at 75. Woodford, who is laureate number 75, started his career with an NSF graduate research fellowship and went on to receive ten more awards from the agency.

The US National Science Foundation has zeroed out the number of new grants in some programme areas of the social sciences and sharply cut others.

Compared with other disciplines, the social sciences are unusually reliant on the NSF. Until late September, the NSF’s social, behavioural and economic sciences (SBE) directorate advertised that it “provides 63% of the funding for all academic work in social and psychological sciences in the US”. That statement has since vanished from the NSF website, and the White House has stated that it wants to eliminate the directorate altogether.

The SBE’s potential dissolution creates uncertainty for entire disciplines. It throws into question projects that the SBE has long supported, including decades-long surveys on US political attitudes and behaviours. Such surveys are “facing an existential crisis right now”, says Brian Schaffner, a political scientist at Tufts University in Medford, Massachusetts.

Without an intervention, “these projects that NSF has funded for a long time will just wither away and die”, says Mark Solovey, a historian at the University of Toronto in Canada, who wrote Social Science for What?, a 2020 book on the history of social science at the agency.

In response to Nature’s request for comment, the NSF said that White House budget request for fiscal year 2027 “does not include continued funding for the Social, Behavioral, and Economic Sciences Directorate” and that the directorate has not been shut down. The agency also said that as part of planning to implement President Trump’s agenda, the “NSF regularly evaluates its portfolio of funding opportunities to ensure alignment with agency priorities”.

The White House has characterized the SBE’s portfolio as “woke” and, in an April budget proposal, said it would eliminate the directorate altogether. Congress has not yet weighed in on the directorate’s fate — but the Trump administration has pressed ahead with cuts to the SBE’s spending all the same.

The SBE’s total spending on new grants fell from an average of US$247 million per fiscal year during 2021–24 to $94 million in 2026. The NSF has allowed the SBE to award new grants only in White House-approved areas, such as artificial intelligence and cognitive science, according to reporting in Science. The SBE now has fewer than a dozen staff members, down from around 50 at the start of Trump’s current term, which began in 2025, and it has no active calls for funding or review panels.

The largest projects funded by the SBE are the ‘big three’ researcher-run surveys, which have been ongoing for decades: the American National Election Studies (ANES), which tracks trends in political engagement and attitudes; the General Social Survey (GSS), a biennial study of the American public’s behaviours, opinions and experiences; and the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, which collects economic data.

White House rolls out AI funding — and signals a new era for US science

White House rolls out AI funding — and signals a new era for US science

These data sets are “a really critical shared public good”, says Pamela Herd, a sociologist at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor and a co-principal investigator on the SBE grant for the GSS. The surveys are also expensive to maintain, in part because they still incorporate face-to-face interviews. Each survey requires several million dollars per year — a funding level out of reach for social-science philanthropy.
