#858. Dylan Sprouse Reveals Mind-Blowing Residual Paycheck From Zack & Cody

Dylan Sprouse shared how much money he actually makes in residuals from The Suite Life of Zack & Cody, which ran for three seasons from 2005 to 2008.

Yes, Dylan Sprouse has a suite life—but it's not from residuals.

The Disney Channel alum got candid about his pay as a former child star, revealing that he hasn't received "a single f--king residual" for starring in The Suite Life of Zack & Cody with his twin brother Cole Sprouse.

"The only residual check I've ever received for The Suite Life at all was a crossover episode with Hannah Montana for five cents," Dylan shared on the Nov. 3 episode of his and Brendan Columbus' Wildmen podcast. "In a time where residuals would have been great, not a single paycheck for being arguably one of the most popular shows on television."

Dylan went on to point out that The Suite Life—which also costarred Brenda Song, Ashley Tisdale, Kim Rhodes and Phill Lewis—was beating The Sopranos in ratings during its three-season run from 2005 to 2008.

"That pops in my head every once in a while," the 34-year-old continued, adding that The Suite Life was "translated into 80 different languages" so it could be broadcasted in different countries. "That's insane."

What's more, according to Dylan's costar Phill, the cast had a "bizarre contract" that allowed Disney to shoot as many episodes of The Suite Life in one calendar year and "call it a season."

"One season, we shot 30 episodes of television," recalled Phill, who played hotel manager Mr. Moseby. "But they called it one season because they didn't have to pay us bumps in between."

E! News has reached out to Disney for comment but hasn't heard back.

Still, Dylan doesn't regret his time on the hit children's show. After all, he made lifelong friends within the cast.

"You were such the force you were on set, as well as still in the bog with us," Dylan told Phill, 58. "I don't think that the show would have felt like the family—nor would it have survived even two years—without you because you were the father of the set."

And that's why Dylan is totally open to working with the original cast again. As he put it, "I still love everyone to death."

But that doesn't mean he'd like to see a Suite Life of Zack & Cody revival.

"I'm seeing all of these older Disney Channel shows get their reboot, but the reboot's always sans this and this person,'" the Under Fire star said. "And I go, 'Well, that's just not the same.'"

Besides, Dylan believes the original show "lives very well" on streaming platforms for "people who are nostalgic" as well as the next generation.

"I was at a Dodger game recently and a kid came up to me," he added. "She was like, 'Did you do a Disney Channel show?' And I was like, 'Well, I used to a while ago.' And she goes, 'It's my dad's favorite show.'"

For more facts and figures on celebrity paychecks, keep reading...

The Jackass star reflected on the "comical" amount of money he was paid for doing death-defying stunts on the MTV series' first season in 2000.

"When it was all said and done, after taxes, I was paid less than $1,500 for the entire first season of Jackass," the daredevil told Playboy in June 2026. "Before the show came out, my sister kicked me out of the house. I was broke, unemployed, and homeless, and a star on this big MTV show."

Oscar winner Jennifer Lawrence was paid $25 million to star in Adam McKay’s ensemble disaster comedy Don’t Look Up. But her costar and fellow Oscar winner Leonardo DiCaprio got $30 million.

“Look, Leo brings in more box office than I do,” Lawrence told Vanity Fair for its’ December 2020/January 2021 issue. “I’m extremely fortunate and happy with my deal. But in other situations, what I have seen—and I’m sure other women in the workforce have seen as well—is that it’s extremely uncomfortable to inquire about equal pay. And if you do question something that appears unequal, you’re told it’s not gender disparity but they can’t tell you what exactly it is.”

Her sanguine attitude was hard-fought: When the disparity between Lawrence’s compensation and that of her male costars for 2013’s American Hustle was revealed in the 2014 Sony email hack, it prompted an industry-wide conversation about the gender pay gap in Hollywood.

"I'm so fortunate to have my job. My problem is not money," Lawrence told the U.K.’s Channel 4 News in 2017. "I wasn't upset that I only got this many millions for a movie. That's ridiculous. I was angry about the unfairness and inequality."

The *NSYNC alum revealed that he and his fellow bandmates JC Chasez, Joey Fatone, Chris Kirkpatrick and Justin Timberlake didn't make much money during their years with the group.

“We had a per diem: $35 a day,” he revealed on The Zach Sang Show in 2026. “Our first check was a $10,000 check after years of No. 1 albums, sellout tours. I don’t know how many millions they made off of merchandise because merchandise was insane.”

“And then they finally gave us a check for $10,000,” he recalled. “You’re like, ‘Oh, thanks.’ We should be grateful for that, been working for free for two, three years now.”

Less comparable to DiCaprio’s salary: The $60,000 “before commissions and taxes” that Jonah Hill was paid for 2013’s The Wolf of Wall Street, while the titular wolf made $10 million.

“They gave me the lowest amount of money possible,” Hill recalled on The Howard Stern Show in 2014. But it was the chance to appear in a Martin Scorsese movie, so the Moneyball alum wanted to get the deal done before anyone could change their mind.

“I would sell my house and give him all my money to work for [Scorsese],” explained Hill, who earned his second Best Supporting Actor nomination for his turn as a squirrelly substance-abusing stockbroker. “This isn't what you make money for. You do 22 Jump Street or you do other things, and you can pay your rent. I would have done anything in the world. I would do it again in a second. This isn't about money. You should do things that you care about."

According to Dylan Sprouse, his residuals from filming The Suite Life of Zack & Cody with twin brother Cole Sprouse is anything but suite.

"The only residual check I've ever received for The Suite Life at all was a crossover episode with Hannah Montana for five cents," the Disney Channel alum shared during a 2026 episode of his Wildmen podcast. "In a time where residuals would have been great, not a single paycheck for being arguably one of the most popular shows on television."

While there's no cash prize for nabbing Dancing With the Stars' mirrorball trophy, “whoever makes it to the finale, you all get paid up until then," Jenna Johnson, who won season 33 with partner Joey Graziadei, shared. "And you do get a nice bonus.”

"If you win," Johnson, who noted pro contracts are dependent on seniority, continued. "it’s not like you get a million dollars. You’re just getting a cute trophy together.” As for those who say farewell to the ballroom early, well, as she explained, "You’re guaranteed until a certain amount of weeks.” According to multiple reports, dancer salaries start at around $1,200 to $1,600 an episode, which can increase to up to of $100,000 per season. (ABC has not confirmed these reports.) On the flip side, celebrities receive a starting salary of $125,000. As they cha-cha further into the competition, stars  receive additional bonuses with the semifinalists and finalists getting paid up to $50,000 extra.

The actress seemingly confirmed that the Friends cast—including Jennifer Aniston, Courtney Cox,David Schwimmer and Matt LeBlanc—get $20 million in residuals per year from the show re-airing, quipping to The Times in April 2026 that if she had to guess why, it's “Because Phoebe Buffay was so great?"

But in actuality, she praised the talents of her costars for their performances.

“I felt I did OK, but Jennifer and Courteney? Amazing,” she raved. “David and Matt? They had me laughing so hard. And then Matthew [Perry]—he was just beyond us all.”

To hear Joe Giudice tell it, his and ex-wife Teresa Giudice's salary for season one of The Real Housewives of New Jersey was nothing to flip over. "We got paid nothing the first season," he detailed on daughter Gia Giudice's Casual Chaos podcast in August 2025. "I'll even say, it was like $25,000. It was ridiculous. But, whatever."

And the ingredientses they put into that initial fame-making season weren't cheap. "I think the first year we had that big party in my great room," the father of four reflected. "I think that show cost me $150,000 the first year."

Oprah Winfrey happily accepted only a little bit of green to star in 1985’s The Color Purple.

“They were only offering $35,000 to be in this film, and it is the best $35,000 I ever earned,” the billionaire media mogul told Essence in 2023. “It changed everything and taught me so much.”

The actress revealed that she made about $20,000 per episode of Two and a Half Men with a 5 percent raise each season, making about $43,000 for one episode in the final season.

When she scored the role of late Tejana singer Selena Quintanilla in the 1997 biopic Selena, Jennifer Lopez became the first Latina actress to earn $1 million for a film.

“I was too young and didn’t know what the hell was going on,” Lopez told Variety in 2019, reflecting on her breakout movie. “It was great they offered me a million dollars. I feel like everyone was making a statement.”

And it paved the way for her to make hundreds of millions more, though sometimes her participation doesn’t cost a thing.

“I do things because I love them,” Lopez explained to GQ in 2019. “I didn't get paid a whole bunch of money for Hustlers. I did it for free and produced it. I bank on myself, you know? Like Jenny From the Block—I do what I love."

Adrien Brody didn’t do The Brutalist for the money. Rather, he took on the role of a Hungarian architect suffering for his art in post-WWII America for $250,000 and won his second Oscar for Best Actor.

“I need a studio movie now, because I’ve poured it all into this,” Brody quipped to Variety, referring to the “barn that looks like a castle” he’s renovating in upstate New York.

“Do you guys know what they pay us?” Pete Davidson cracked to New York magazine when asked ahead of Saturday Night Live's 50th anniversary special how he spent his money when he was first hired at the age of 20 in 2014. “It’s like three grand an episode, so I think I got dinner.”

Interestingly, the salaries have remained proportional for SNL newcomers, with season one stars John Belushi, Jane Curtin, Gilda Radner, Dan Aykroyd and Chevy Chase reportedly earning $750 an episode back in 1975. Which was roughly equivalent to $3,300 in 2014, according to the Consumer Price Index Inflation calculator. (Though the $750 of 1975 is $4,428 in 2025.)

While Kenan Thompson makes a lot more than $3,000 per episode of SNL now that he’s in his record 22nd season, the former Nickelodeon star had to start somewhere.

“That first commercial when they paid me, it was $800,” the All That alum revealed in Demi Lovato‘s 2024 documentary Child Star. “I was 12 so that may as well have been a million dollars."

It turns out Gilmore Girls’ status as a beloved rewatchable classic is literally priceless.

“There really are no residuals on Netflix,” Lauren Graham, who played Lorelai Gilmore for seven seasons and then reprised the role for 2016’s Gilmore Girls: A Year in the Life, said on Jimmy Kimmel Live in March 2025. “But I’ve been paid in love and appreciation.”

Feeling not so appreciated, Tommy Dorfman got specific about her 13 Reasons Why paycheck during the 2023 SAG-AFTRA strike—which was prompted in part (as was the WGA strike) by streamers like Netflix not making it a practice to pay additional compensation to cast and crew once a show had become a big hit.

"my earnings for the entire first season of 13 reasons why were $29,953.24 prior to agency and manager fees (20%) and taxes," Dorfman wrote on Threads July 24. "8 episodes over six months." She continued, “i did all of the promo and had KEY ART for this show, flew round trip from NYC to SF to shoot for every episode, was kept for days without pay/working. i barely qualified for insurance."

And, Dorfman added, “within the first 28 days of release, the show's season 1 garnered a total of 476 million view hours. this is why we strike."

Without naming names or numbers, Dax Shepard told fellow Parenthood alum Lauren Graham when she appeared on his podcast that he knew he made “among the lowest of all the actors” on their NBC drama, which ran for six seasons.

But, the Armchair Expert host stressed that he did not mind.

“Every job I had ever had in my life prior to Parenthood, I made a point to find out what everyone was making,” he said. “I'd always figure it out—either a conversation where I get it out of them or I backchannel through an agent."

So he made a point to purposely not seek out such info about his Parenthood family, which helped with enjoying the experience even when he did get an inkling of where he was on the pay pyramid.

“I got a dollar for writing the script,” George Clooney told the Los Angeles Times in 2005 about the financial strings he pulled to get his film Good Night, and Good Luck made. “I had to endorse my check for directing and turn in my acting salary. [Actor, cowriter and coproducer Grant Heslov] and I each made a buck for doing it.”

His labor of love about CBS News journalist Edward R. Murrow speaking truth to power in the 1950s had legs, though: Making his Broadway debut, Clooney wrapped his months-long stint playing Murrow in a stage adaptation of the film  in June 2025. And with the play having grossed a Broadway record (for a nonmusical) $3.3 million during a preview week before it officially opened April 3, he made a lot more than $1.

For his chilling turn as Patrick Bateman in 2000’s American Psycho, Christian Bale was paid “the absolute minimum they were legally allowed to pay me” because no one in the production really wanted to hire him except director Mary Harron, the Welsh actor told GQ in 2022.

He made so little, Bale shared, that he remembered “sitting in the makeup trailer and the makeup artists were laughing at me because I was getting paid less than any of them.”

No, the Game of Thrones cast didn't get paid $300,000 per episode, according to Emilia Clarke.

“We didn’t earn that much," she told Variety in 2026. "Can you imagine? I’d have been driving a couple of Porsches!"

However, the actress—who played Daenerys Targaryen for eight seasons between 2011 and 2019—noted that the money she made throughout the HBO show did provide her with enough financial security to pay off her parents’ mortgage.

His uncle may have been Rico, but Jon Heder confirmed in 2010 that he was “initially” only paid $1,000 for Napoleon Dynamite.

After the irreverent comedy became a sleeper hit, he was able to renegotiate for a piece of the profits, telling the New Zealand Herald, “They went a little bit higher.”

Djimon Hounsou said he’s “definitely underpaid” in Hollywood despite his prestigious list of credits, including Amistad and Blood Diamond.

"I've been in this business and making films now over two decades," the Beninese actor told CNN’s Larry Madowo in January 2025. "And still—with two Oscar nominations and been in many big blockbuster films—and yet I’m still struggling financially to make a living."

Rebel Wilson detailed in her 2024 memoir Rebel Rising that she was paid $3,500 to do Bridesmaids, “a fee that I then had to pay directly to the Screen Actors Guild to join the union. So really, I got paid nothing.”

Still, she wrote, the experience was “everything!”

And the Australian actress’ star rose ever a-ca higher, with her fee going from the SAG minimum scale of $65,000 for 2012’s Pitch Perfect to $10 million for 2017’s Pitch Perfect 3. Wilson wrote that she raked in $20 million total for the threequel, Isn’t It Romantic and The Hustle, though—reality alert—she “lost almost 50 percent to taxes, 10 percent to agents and 5 percent” to her lawyer. But even after those obligations and paying her publicist, business manager and assistant, Wilson “netted what to me was an absolute fortune.”

In late 2017, Ellen Pompeo negotiated a new Grey’s Anatomy contract for $575,000 per episode, a seven-figure signing bonus and two full backend equity points worth an estimated $6 million to $7 million.

“I’m 48 now, so I’ve finally gotten to the place where I’m OK asking for what I deserve, which is something that comes only with age,” Pompeo told The Hollywood Reporter in 2018. “Because I’m not the most ‘relevant’ actress out there. I know that’s the industry perception because I’ve been this character for 14 years. But the truth is, anybody can be good on a show season one and two. Can you be good 14 years later? Now, that’s a f--kin’ skill.”

Reflecting more recently on how she always made less than costar Patrick Dempsey, even though she was the Grey in question, Pompeo said she didn’t begrudge him his money.

But, she said on a March 2025 episode of Call Her Daddy, “Just being that I was the namesake of the show, I deserved the same and that was harder to get. I wasn't salty about him getting what he got. I was salty that they didn't value me as much as they valued him and they never will.”

Jamie Lee Curtis recalled getting paid $2,000 a week—so $8,000 in total—for 1978’s Halloween, her movie debut. “I mean,” she told Rotten Tomatoes in 2018, “nobody got paid, anything.”

Yet while the scream queen earned four figures, director John Carpenter’s friend Nick Castle felt like a king making $25 per day to share the role of Michael Myers. (It’s Anthony Moran whose face you see when the killer’s mask comes off for a freaky second, and editor Tommy Lee Wallace also logged screentime as Michael.)

“That was a lot at the time!” Castle, who attended film school at USC with Carpenter, told Vanity Fair in 2018. “You have to remember: My interest in doing the film was being on set, so I could demystify the experience of filmmaking and directing. I expected to hang around the set for no money. But hey, $25 per day, and all I had to do was wear a rubber mask.”

Taraji P. Henson earned a Best Supporting Actress Oscar nomination for 2008’s The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, but years later she was still fired up by the $150,000 she accepted to be in the movie—after producers rejected the $500,000 quote she brought to the table.

As for the film’s leads Brad Pitt and Cate Blanchett, “You don’t hear a lot of $20 million quotes anymore, but at this time that was happening,” Henson said on the Ladies First With Laura Brown podcast in 2021. “And rightfully so—I’m not saying they shouldn’t have paid Cate and Brad what they deserved.”

But, she continued, “I’m bringing a certain amount to the seat too and I felt like what I was asking at that time in my career was fair, was fair to the ticket sales that I would contribute to this big film. Wouldn’t do it.” Henson was “gutted” when they offered $100,000, she recalled. “When it was all said and done I got $150,000, but I had to swallow my pride, baby.”

Breaking it down, “I know people go, ‘$150,000, that’s a lot of money!’” Henson acknowledged. “I don’t ever want people to think that I’m ungrateful because that is not me.” But, she calculated, “Uncle Sam is going to take 50 percent of that, so now you’re left with, what? $75,000. Now before Uncle Sam takes the money, I have to pay my team before taxes, 30 percent. So once Uncle Sam takes his 75, then I got another 30 that’s coming off of that 75, so I may have made $40,000?”

While Blanchett has made plenty of money over the years, it didn’t all come from playing royal elf Galadriel in The Lord of the Rings franchise, though it grossed $2.9 billion at the worldwide box office.

“Are you kidding me? No,” she retorted on Watch What Happens Live in August 2024 when Andy Cohen guessed LOTR was her biggest paycheck. “No one got paid anything to do that movie…I mean, I basically got free sandwiches, and I got to keep my ears.”

They weren’t paid a precious amount, that is. Orlando Bloom, who played elven warrior Legolas, shared on The Howard Stern Show in 2023 that he made $175,000 for the whole trilogy.

#855. Why Ramayana: Rise of a Legend Part 2 Will Premiere in 2028, Not 2027

While fans prepare to meet Ram and Sita in Ramayana: Rise of a Legend Part One, premiering Nov. 5, producer Namit Malhotra told E! News why they are waiting an additional year to release the sequel.

Rama's journey to Lanka will take longer than anticipated.

Though moviegoers will meet the prince of Ayodhya (Ranbir Kapoor) and his wife Sita (Sai Pallavi) in the first part of Ramayana: Rise of a Legend—in theaters Nov. 5—some questions will remain unanswered until its sequel, which is now slated to premiere in 2028 rather than 2027.

"When we announced the first part, we were thinking of it primarily as an Indian film going to the world," producer Namit Malhotra told E! News in an exclusive interview. "Through the evolution of the film, we've now come to a place where we actually have two master versions."

He noted that dubbing the first part in English required a separate edit and a rewrite of the OG script from Hindi "so that it can be presented in its own original form."

Part one follows a young Ram—the eldest of three half-brothers: Lakshmana, Bharata and Shatrughna—as he is chosen as the Hindu god Vishnu's avatar to take down the demon king Ravana (Yash). However, that conflict comes later.

The prince, an archer, continues training as a soldier before marrying Sita. While Ram lives out his fairytale romance his dad, King Dasharatha, ultimately exiles him for 14 years at the behest of Bharata's mom, Queen Kaikeyi. (One of Dasharatha's three wives, Kaikeyi demanded her son take the throne.)

Ram doesn't leave alone, however. Sita and Lakshmana join him on this journey, fighting demons along the way.

With such an unforgettable ending to the epic—which Diwali commemorates each year—Malhotra knew their team would need another year to work on part two.

"We want to take a little bit more time to make sure that when we present the grand finale," he explained, "that we have a little bit more time to do the same thing that we did on part one."

"That extra year, I think, is what I genuinely believe we need to do justice to a film of this size," he explained. "Especially when you see part two coming in, that will be a whole other story of what happens there."

After all, the sequel will follow Ram's journey to find Sita after she was kidnapped by Ravana.

"We didn't want to do a rush job or get ahead of ourselves," he added, "and we wanted to make sure that we delivered the finale in as much grandeur as it deserves."

Meanwhile, Kapoor was focused on making sure he and Pallavi gave Ram and Sita's loving dynamic the grandeur it deserved, too.

"The relationship between Lord Ram and Sita is not really about expressing everything you feel, but actually just looking at each other and understanding," he told E!. "It also tells us that love is not about being together when times are good, but also standing by each other when you know times are hard."

"In the entire story of the Ramayana, I think it's Sita Ma's character who actually experiences the greatest loss," the Animal actor reflected. "Sita sacrifices everything to be with Lord Ram. There's so much good learnings of love, of sacrifice, of compassion, of togetherness. I hope that it resonates with today's youth all across the world, not just Indians."

#853. Are De Zerbi's Spurs finding elusive consistency?

Spurs revival continues with victory over 10-man Crystal Palace

The long wait is over. After almost 21 months, Tottenham Hotspur have won three Premier League games in succession again.

Spurs cruised to victory on Saturday against Crystal Palace, who were reduced to 10 men after 13 minutes when striker Jean-Philippe Mateta was sent off for an ill-judged lunge at Micky van de Ven.

It means Tottenham have moved into the dizzy heights of the top half of the table.

Archie Gray and Jan Paul van Hecke scored as Spurs built on a platform established by their first league win of the season at home to Coventry City, then fortified by the outstanding victory at Chelsea - only Spurs' second league triumph at Stamford Bridge in 36 years.

But the prevailing mood inside the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium before kick-off against Palace, undoubtedly shaped by the past, was that the visit of a struggling side represented a banana skin rather than an opportunity.

Tottenham's players weren't having that, though. Not a bit of it. Instead, Spurs grasped gratefully at the helping hand offered by Mateta's recklessness to end up convincing winners.

Three straight wins represent riches indeed. The last time this happened for Tottenham was in February 2025, more than 600 days ago.

Three wins is as many as Spurs had in their previous 26 league games combined, in which they drew 10 and lost 13, going back to midway through last season.

And, if a further indicator was needed as to just how poor Spurs have been in recent times, this is the first occasion when they have recorded back-to-back home wins in the league for two years.

This latest sequence represents consistency of the sort that has eluded Spurs in recent years, the previous incarnation being the consistency of regular defeats and two successive 17th-place finishes in the Premier League.

Tottenham boss Roberto de Zerbi gives his post-match verdict

We are witnessing a significant mood shift at Spurs, reflected inside this magnificent arena since the psychological barrier of the vital first league win was crossed against Coventry.

Head coach Roberto de Zerbi told BBC Sport's Match Of The Day: "The passion we showed - we didn't lose the focus, the concentration. We made an incredible reaction when we lost the ball.

"We could have scored more goals, but we created many chances. We have to be more nasty, especially in the last third of the match, especially in the finishing. I'm happy because I knew before this would be a tough game."

De Zerbi pleaded for patience for his big summer acquisitions, with midfield duo Sandro Tonali, a Â£100m arrival from Newcastle United, and Â£85m signing Mateus Fernandes, who came from West Ham United, both starting slowly.

While any optimistic verdict on Spurs in recent times always comes with natural caution attached, the expensive pair are now showing signs of why De Zerbi was prepared to pay such prices to make them part of his transformation.

Tonali started to come to life against Coventry City and here he was pivotal with his running power, physicality and creation. Fernandes was lively throughout, always looking for the opening, the pass that could make a difference.

And once again, to the usual rapturous reception after his long injury absence, Dejan Kulusevski delivered a lively cameo as substitute, a real threat as he also forced a fine save from Palace keeper Dean Henderson.

There is a sense that something is finally stirring at Spurs, that the Â£300m spent in the summer might just reap a reward â as you would expect for such a lavish outlay.

The statistics confirmed Spurs' superiority, although Crystal Palace battled gamely with their numerical disadvantage, never looking like a side who had given up on head coach Pierre Sage, although he will now come under increasing scrutiny as they lie in the bottom three with only two wins from nine league games.

Spurs had 34 shots and faced just two, the biggest shot difference (32) they have had against any opponent since such Opta records began in 2003-04.

It is also the biggest for any side since Liverpool had 36 shots against four from Wolverhampton Wanderers in May 2024.

Spurs also had 79.4% possession, their second highest on record in a Premier League match after they had 80.2% against Newcastle United in August 2019.

Tottenham's Â£100m summer signing Sandro Tonali, seen here congratulating Jan Paul van Hecke after his goal, is now exerting his influence

Spurs pile pressure on Sage as 10-man Palace are beaten

It all left De Zerbi delighted as he talked with renewed optimism and ambition, saying: "Listen, we are Tottenham. We can't forget to be ambitious, to be hungry, to win games in a row, and to make our fans happy.

"At the same time, we can't forget two weeks ago where we have been in the table, to change the last two to three seasons of this club. Three games in a row is not enough. We have to keep this behaviour, this spirit. This condition to prepare every game in the same way.

"After the international break, we spoke together honestly, and decided to change the mood quickly because in football, you can't ask for time, especially if you have good players like we have. I think nothing has changed, but the mood, spirit, the relationship with the players are totally different."

The mood has shifted and - for now - the curve looks to be moving in an upward direction for Spurs and De Zerbi.

#851. Is double drop from the Premier League becoming more common?

Are Burnley set to follow a growing trend?

One day Leicester were playing Liverpool in the Premier League, then within 15 months it was Notts County, Burton Albion and MK Dons in League One.

It is a path of back-to-back relegations to the third tier of English football which was exceptionally rare. Now statistically it is becoming more common.

With Burnley marooned in the Championship relegation zone, they could be the third team in three years to suffer the double drop.

For the 1,450 Burnley supporters who made the trip to Lincoln City last weekend, the threat is all too real.

Head coach Nicky Hayen was never likely to survive a 4-1 defeat by a Lincoln team who were in non-league football 10 years ago.

With Diego Lopez appointed as Burnley's new chief football officer, and Fabio Celestini installed as their new boss, the Clarets must now hope for a change in fortunes.

Is the Championship becoming ever-more competitive as well-run clubs like Lincoln make an impact?

Or it simply a case of clubs from the Premier League imploding after relegation?

Fifteen years ago, the suggestion a top-flight club could be relegated in successive seasons was unthinkable.

After all, in the first 20 seasons of the Premier League it happened just the once.

That was to Swindon Town, and even then there were special circumstances.

The Robins finished fourth bottom of the second tier in 1994-95 but were relegated because of the rebalancing of the divisions to reduce the Premier League to 20 teams.

In any other season they would not have suffered the double drop.

As such, it could be argued that Wolves were the first team to suffer a double drop from the Premier League after being relegated in 2011-12.

Since then it has happened four times in 14 seasons.

Or, after Sunderland went down in 2016-18, three times in nine seasons.

And then back-to-back seasons with Luton and Leicester.

Meanwhile, Wigan and Portsmouth were relegated to League One after a second season in the Championship, Leeds and Sheffield Wednesday after a third.

For Wolves, Sunderland and Leicester there was considerable turmoil on and off the pitch which contributed to their demise.

Burney fans may fear there are similarities at Turf Moor.

During their double drop descent, Wolves - who remarkably suffered a treble drop to the bottom tier in the 1980s - burned through four managers and made a series of poor transfers.

Sunderland did so with the ignominy of being the only club to finish bottom of both divisions, winning just 13 of 84 league matches.

The Black Cats had been in the top flight for 10 seasons - though they had only reached the 40-point barrier, usually the target to remain in the division, three times.

Leicester's relegation to League One was a direct result of poor boardroom decisions, with a six-point deduction for breaching profit and sustainability regulations ultimately sealing their fate. The Foxes finished 23rd in the Championship, five points from safety.

It took Sunderland four years to return to the Championship, and such is the turmoil at Leicester an immediate promotion looks unlikely. Russell Martin's Leicester side sit 11th in League One, with the club up for sale.

"Despite the fact we've seen Luton and Leicester suffer back-to-back relegations in recent years, I don't see it as a trend that will continue," former Watford and Reading midfielder Jobi McAnuff, now an EFL pundit, told BBC Sport.

"For both of those clubs, in my opinion, it was a case of mismanagement of the playing squad.

"From Luton's perspective, there were a few players there who maybe felt an entitlement to stay in the Premier League. They didn't readjust to being back at the Championship, where most of their players had actually been previously.

"And for Leicester City, they kept hold of too many that didn't really want to be there and then obviously weren't equipped to deal with a relegation battle."

While Luton may have got their recruitment wrong, they were much more responsibly run compared to the other double drop clubs.

The Hatters' progress off the pitch remains progressive rather than regressive, with work advancing on a new 25,000-capacity stadium at Power Court which is due to be completed for the start of 2028-29.

The fine line for success is shown by Luton's relegation from the Championship in 2024-25. They went down because of their inferior goal difference compared to Hull City, with the Tigers then promoted to the Premier League the following season.

Burnley supporters have been protesting against the ownership of Alan Pace's ALK Capital for much of the season

Burnley had earned a reputation as the archetypal yo-yo club - relegated from or promoted to the top division in each of the past five seasons.

But after a leveraged buyout by Alan Pace's ALK Capital in 2020, the Clarets were carrying Â£142m in loans in the 2024-25 accounts - the year they went up - which was the highest debt level in the Championship.

This week Burnley set a new English league record for the longest run without a home win. When they host Portsmouth on Saturday, it will be 378 days since their last home victory.

Being humbled by a well-run, up-and-coming club like Lincoln, with far fewer resources but savvy ownership, will not be lost on Burnley supporters.

Burnley's total revenue for 2024-25 was Â£71.7m, which dwarfed Lincoln's Â£7.81m.

The Clarets then received Â£48m in parachute payments. Lincoln can expect about Â£5.5m in solidarity funding.

Off the pitch there should be no contest, but football is not played purely on balance sheets.

In its State of the Game report, published earlier this month, the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) said a new financial deal between the Premier League and the EFL must "reduce the distortive impact that parachute payments have on financial incentives within the Championship".

The solution is merit payments, which would mirror the Premier League's model of prize money by final league position.

At present, every club in the Championship receives the same payment, regardless of where they finish.

"The amount of money paid in parachute payments will reduce and the amount of money going into the Championship will vastly increase," IFR chair David Kogan said.

"The delta between parachute payment clubs and non-parachute payment clubs is going to significantly reduce, which makes the Championship a much more competitive league."

Parachute payments are paid to clubs relegated from the Premier League to help them adjust to the financial realities of the second tier - Â£48m in year one, then Â£39m in year two,

Could this make the double drop more common as the revenue gap closes? Much will depend upon just how "significantly" the gap is closed.

The IFR report found that parachute payment clubs were more than four times more likely to be promoted. In 2024-25, four clubs were in receipt and they were almost 27 points better off, and filled the top three places (with Luton relegated).

"If you look at the numbers of teams that go back up or finish in the top places, there's a huge correlation between those clubs and the ones that are parachute payment clubs," McAnuff said.

"Even with a reduction in parachute payments, I still feel that advantage will prove to be massively significant for those teams.â ââ ââ "

It may yet be that Burnley escape the double drop, that the financial advantage of parachute payments outweighs poor decision-making.

But the double drop has generally become far more common. And that should concern any club that gets relegated and is not prepared for life in the Championship.

#850. France: Hundreds arrested after nationwide protests

The French government says more than 1,000 people were arrested following nationwide protests on Saturday. Police and elite security forces were out in force across the country as clashes broke out.

This blog is now closed. Thank you for reading.

You can read all our updates on the protests and unrest in France and other parts of Europe on October 24 and 25, 2026, below.

Marine Le Pen launched her fourth bid to become president of France on Sunday with a plea to "French patriots" to back her and her far-right National Rally (RN) in spring elections.

The grande dame of the far-right, Le Pen delivered an impassioned invocation of French spirit in Orleans, calling for "a renaissance" of the country's virtues and stressing its rich creative and intellectual history.

She blasted "Little Marquis Macron" and the state of France under his stewardship — both domestically and internationally — offering a fiery outline of the need to restore order, but also civility in the country, alongside promises of maintaining French (nuclear) defense and judicial sovereignty.

Le Pen said "we'll protect our public spaces so that they can remain places full of life and mutual respect" and cited civility as the surest way to keep violence out of society.

She praised regionalism over globalism or supranationalism in the form of the European Union (EU), and spoke of the need to defend freedom and the "French way of life," making clear that, "In France, you live like the French."

Le Pen recalled General Charles de Gaulle several times throughout her speech, emphasizing the historic importance of the moment when it comes to securing the promise of the future.

After ending her remarks with a full-throated "Vive la France!," a relieved-looking Le Pen was joined on stage by heir apparent Jordan Bardella and party members for a rousing rendition of the national anthem under the campaign slogan, "Pour la France La Renaissance."

Amid the latest demonstrations, what's driving the unrest, and could a broader youth-led protest movement be taking shape?

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

French unions and protest groups have called for fresh demonstrations on October 31 and a nationwide strike on November 5 to maintain pressure on the government.

The left-wing Solidaires union federation said anger over wages, living costs and public services was bringing together students, workers, firefighters and other groups.

"We see an aggregation of anger," Solidaires co-leader Murielle Guilbert told broadcaster BFM TV.

The SUD Education teaching union said it would join the October 31 demonstrations. The larger CGT union is set to decide during the week.

The Yellow Vests movement also called for rallies, including sit-ins outside town halls and the National Assembly.

The government has opened talks with unions and student representatives, but protest leaders say its proposals are inadequate.

French authorities detained 1,314 people during nationwide protests on Saturday, according to a provisional Interior Ministry tally.

The ministry said 53 police officers and other security personnel were injured, firefighters responded to 75 fires and 24 businesses were looted. It did not provide a figure for injured protesters.

Clashes broke out in cities including Paris, Marseille, Bordeaux, Toulouse and Tours, with police using tear gas. The ministry blamed groups including radical far-left activists for confrontations along or near protest routes.

Authorities counted 410,000 participants at 289 demonstrations and gatherings, down from 550,000 a week earlier. Other estimates put Saturday's turnout as high as 800,000.

The reported arrests and violence were substantially lower than on October 17, when authorities recorded 2,628 detentions and 1,144 injured security personnel.

The ministry said several investigations had been opened and described the subsequent night as calm.

With Saturday's protest over, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez reported nearly 1,000 arrests.

The number is expected to rise as security officials tally up the day's events, Nunez added.

"Multiple lootings have been averted," he said.

While some clashes between protesters and police were reported in many French cities, the scope of the unrest was much smaller compared to the protests last Saturday, which saw buildings defaced and burned, and some 1,500 shops looted across the country.

Nunez previously put the number of people arrested last weekend at 2,700.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Some 410,000 people marched across France on Saturday, according to the country's interior ministry, as the country braced for a possible repeat of violence seen last weekend.

In Paris alone, at least 110,000 ‌people turned out to denounce rising ⁠living ⁠costs and growing inequality.

Police were out in force in major French cities. While rallies in Paris and Marseille were mostly peaceful, clashes between protesters and police were reported in towards the evening.

Riot police in Paris fired tear gas and water cannons at some 500 hooded youths before they eventually dispersed. In Marseille, youths blocked roads by setting trash cans on fire. They threw rocks and bottles at security forces.

Clashes were also reported in the cities of Lyon, Bordeaux, Grenoble, Clermont-Ferrand, Lille, Rennes, Nantes and Toulouse.

France is known for its protest culture, where demonstration is considered a bedrock value.

Altercations between the police and demonstrators are by and large part of the French protest ritual.

What we are seeing could even be considered a relatively calm end-of-demonstration situation, Lisa Louis, who is in Paris, said.

Meanwhile, security guards were deployed in Milan on Saturday amid demonstrations against the rising cost of living.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni ordered 500 soldiers to be dispatched to the city, in addition to about 5,000 police and other law enforcement personnel there.

But the protests in the large Italian city were less unruly than last weekend, when looters ransacked businesses near the central Duomo area. Around 3,000 people rallied in Milan, with another smaller demonstration taking place in Rome.

As the day went on (and largely toward the end of demonstrations in many cities), clashes occurred between protesters and the authorities during the demonstrations across France.

The French interior ministry said it estimates 410,000 people to have taken part in protest throughout France today.

Demonstrations were set to take place in Paris and Marseille but protesters took to the streets in other cities for rallies like Lyon and Nantes.

There were reports about clashes between protesters and police in several cities, including Paris.

There were protests in the city of Lyon, in the east-central part of France, where police used tear gas to disperse protesters wearing masks.

There are also reports about clashes in Marseille, where police fired tear gas to disperse crowds.

About 550,000 people attended demonstrations throughout the country last weekend.

The mood over the past few days in France felt almost a bit apocalyptic. Business owners told me they were worried more looting might lie ahead, after gangs of individuals had ransacked and destroyed at least 3,000 shops across the country last weekend.

"Some of us are planning to buy weapons to defend ourselves, in case the pillagers come back. One day, there's going to be a tragedy — for sure," Jonathan Siad, owner of a tobacco shop in Paris, said to me.

Other store owners were too afraid to talk to us in front of the camera – they worried criminals might see the interview and target their shop.

Residents told me they would try to avoid the area where the demonstration was taking place. Only to add that they hoped the situation wouldn't escalate like last week, when even places far away from the actual marches became hotspots of clashes between the police and protesters.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez had admitted on Monday a "loss of control" last Saturday. The authorities thus increased the number of police deployed across France by 10,000 to 70,000 this Saturday.

First clashes between protesters and the police started to occur in the late afternoon in several cities across France such as Marseille, Lyon and Paris.

But for now, the much feared mass looting and ransacking doesn't seem to be happening. The situation is nowhere near the total chaos Paris and other cities like Marseille experienced last Saturday.

"Last weekend, our neighborhood resembled a war zone with gangs roaming the area. Today, it's completely empty apart from police with their vans," Yassaman Metghalchi, co-owner of a jewelry shop in the city center of Paris that got looted last Saturday, told me.

"All of our neighbors feel reassured – although the night is still young and we need to wait and see what will happen," she added.

Paris police say 110,000 protesters were on the streets in the city on Saturday. The anti-government "Yellow Vest" movementteamed up with aggrieved school students for this round of demonstrations.

The CGT trade union, meanwhile, said 800,000 participated in protests across France, with 250,000 people taking part in Paris.

Saturday's protesters were limited by Parisian authorities to the city's southeastern edge, away from the center.

Authorities prepared to help the protesters march safely from the Place d'Italie in the 13th arrondissement on the left bank of the Seine River to Porte de Vincennes which lies further away on the right bank.

A post on X by Paris Police Prefecture showed the Porte d'Italie from the sky ahead of the march.

French news agency AFP reported clashes in Paris after the demonstrations.

The French police used tear gas in response to protests in the southeastern city of Lyon. Use of tear gas was also reported in the cities of Lille, Toulouse and Nantes.

In Orleans, south of Paris, protesters also came out to the streets against a two-day congress held in the city of Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally party.

According to polls, Le Pen is the frontrunner in France's presidential elections next year.

#849. Harry Kane’s Ballon d’Or party gives way to anxiety-filled hangover for Bayern Munich | Andy Brassell

Dortmund did not read the script, remaining level on points with the defending champions at the top of the table

It was the moment they had all been … not so much waiting for, but planning, pushing and yearning for. In the videos that announce the starting lineup on the giant scoreboard before kick-off, every Bayern Munich player turns to face the camera with their personal salute, greeting or goal celebration, the playful progression from the standard folding of arms. Except on Saturday evening, the No 9 turned around smiling, and cradling the golden trophy.

In the midweek DFB Pokal stroll against Magdeburg there had been a salute, the players welcoming Harry Kane on to the pitch with a guard of honour to commemorate his Ballon d’Or victory two nights before. This, however, was the real party, the moment where the England captain’s and Bayern’s successful union and the apex it has reached was celebrated in front of a global audience. There was every reason to believe it would be a full and satisfying victory lap, even in Der Klassiker, with proper competition so often bringing the best out of the Rekordmeister.

Dortmund, however, did not read the script. Neither did the football gods. Kane was not completely neutered in this and laid on yet another assist, nodding across goal to present Dayot Upamecano a second goal in successive Bundesliga games That looked like the winner until Fábio Silva’s 89th-minute equaliser for the visitors. Yet in between, there was frustration for the man who has walked on water since arriving in Munich. He clattered a penalty which could have made it 2-0 against the crossbar and hit the post from point-blank range when he could have made it 3-1, after Serhou Guirassy’s first equaliser and the Upamecano strike that put Bayern back in front.

Three years ago on Wednesday, Kane hit a hat-trick in his first Klassiker in a 4-0 win at Signal Iduna Park. Despite the cliche that BVB are Bayern’s bunnies, the champions have not had it all their own way in this fixture. This was Kane’s fourth Klassiker at the Allianz Arena, and Bayern have only won one of them. Many of those watching from around the world who tuned in to see Kane lift his personal trophy would have expected a subsequent procession to victory but having arrived level on points at the top of the table, Dortmund were able to leave Bavaria in the same position.

This was, as Ruhr Nachrichten’s Kevin Pinnow put it, “much more than just a point” for Dortmund. It was not a signal they are Bayern’s equal but a sign they could roll with the punches, that they could show guts and enterprise and find solutions, from the switch to a back four that blind-sided their hosts to the energy and daring in midfield, exemplified by Jobe Bellingham’s best performance since he arrived last year. The young Englishman is a symbol of the good Niko Kovac has done since arriving at the club, a combination of patience and high demand. The coach insisted earlier this year that Bellingham, despite a lack of numerical reward, was progressing ahead of schedule and this, finally was the proof. He might even have put BVB in front in the first half, but had a goal ruled out as the offside Carney Chukwuemeka – who also excelled – inadvertently stumbled into Jonas Urbig in the Bayern goal. “He is someone for the big stake,” enthused the sporting director, Ole Book. “He showed that today.”

SV Elversberg 4-1 Mainz, Augsburg 1-2 Freiburg, Mönchengladbach 0-0 Paderborn, Schalke 0-2 RB Leipzig, Werder 2-0 Hoffenheim, Leverkusen 2-4 VfB Stuttgart, Bayern 2-2 Dortmund, Union Berlin 1-1 Köln, Eintracht Frankfurt 3-1 Hamburg

Yet as worthy as Dortmund were, little went for Bayern. The bad luck was not limited to plural pinging of aluminium and the effects will last for longer than Monday morning. Already without Vincent Kompany, who will not be rushed back into action after his recent hospitalisation with his assistant, Aaron Danks, holding the fort, the injury list is getting out of hand. Danks went into this fixture without Luis Díaz, Manuel Neuer and Jamal Musiala and lost a further three forward players during the course of the evening.

Ismael Saibari injured his ankle ligaments in a collision with Gregor Kobel and has already had surgery, with the recovery to last at least three months. Serge Gnabry is expected to miss several weeks with a hamstring injury he picked up and, worst of all, Michael Olise went down off the ball with what appeared to be a knee problem in the closing minutes. Bayern will go into this week’s Champions League game with Atlético Madrid – surely the last game they would wish to face with a banged-up squad – with only two senior forward players available, Kane and the 18-year-old Lennart Karl.

Karl still almost won the game for the hosts, bending a shot from range against the top of the crossbar in stoppage time He might have many other chances to make himself the hero in the games to come. As will Kane, again and again. We will see quite how the immediate post-Ballon d’Or period will unfold. One of Kane’s key characteristics throughout his career has been his relentless availability, but part of his ascension to his best-ever self has been based on Kompany’s ability to rest his star turn and keep him fresh. With the current plethora of injuries, Danks is unlikely to have the same luxury.

It is impossible to talk about turning points in the season on Halloween. Yet Kane will be loading Bayern on his broad shoulders ever more than before, and Dortmund’s next challenge is to be brave enough to try to take advantage.

If Sebastian Hoeness and his Stuttgart team were going to lift themselves out of a crisis of confidence it was always going to be not by eking out a gritty result, but by blasting their way back to health, and that is what they did at Leverkusen, winning 4-2 in a fixture that has been one of the Bundesliga’s must-watch match-ups of recent seasons. For all their attacking punch, Hoeness and company arrived having lost four out of five on the back of some profligate finishing. Here they were clinical in a testy game against a Werkself team who had chances of their own. “Unfortunately, we can’t play Leverkusen 34 times,” lamented the Champions League joint top scorer Ermedin Demirovic, who scored twice. “They’re always heated and exciting matches because both teams play with attacking intent.”

Leipzig strolled to a 2-0 win at an impotent Schalke – still yet to score a home goal – before facing Manchester City, an important step to Martín Demichelis shoring up his position. The Norwegian winger Antonio Nusa, who scored one and made one, excelled.

Niclas Füllkrug was at it again for Werder Bremen, after an attempted midweek DFB Pokal rescue act at his old club Borussia Dortmund, scoring twice to bring Werder level before their hopes were dashed by a late Marcel Sabitzer winner. The centre-forward blasted the northerners into the lead on Saturday against Hoffenheim, setting up a win that pushes them into the top five. It was his seventh straight Bundesliga game scoring, equalling the legendary Rudi Völler’s record from 1982-83. “I’m truly speechless,” said the goalkeeper Karl Hein, whose huge clearance set the goal up. “It’s a privilege to have him with us.” Even with his plan to revitalise Germany and make the squad younger, it is hard to see how Jürgen Klopp can omit Füllkrug when he announces his next Germany squad on Thursday.

#848. 'We fell behind' - what does new San Siro deal mean for AC Milan and Inter?

Why time is running out for the iconic San Siro

When AC Milan and city rivals Inter jointly revealed the design of their planned new stadium on Thursday, one thing stood out in particular - the name.

The 71,500-seater arena the clubs aim to share from 2031 onwards, replacing the iconic San Siro, will be called the Generali Stadium.

Generali is an Italian insurance company, and the firm has agreed to pay about 650m euros (Â£542m) for naming rights through to 2052.

The length and value of the agreement makes it one of the most lucrative naming-rights deals in sports history.

Stadium naming rights are, of course, nothing new in elite football. The champions of England and Germany both play in arenas built in the 21st century that have always been known by their sponsors' name, and plenty more stadiums across the continent have been partly financed by revenue from naming rights.

But in recent years, some clubs have struggled to sell them.

It was thought that both Tottenham Hotspur and West Ham would look to sell the rights to their new stadiums' names, but as yet neither have. Liverpool aimed to sell the name of a new stand they built in 2016 but no such deal has been agreed.

So, what do these stadium plans mean for AC Milan and Inter, what underpins the viability of expensive new football grounds, and what impact do culture and history have?

AC Milan and Inter are owned by separate US-based investment firms and in the joint announcement described the Generali Stadium as "a new home for generations of supporters, and a destination designed to contribute to the cultural, economic and urban development of the city".

The demolition of San Siro has been discussed for decades, and the clubs believe its deterioration and lack of modern features are significant reasons behind their progressive fall lower down the pecking order at the top of European football.

The new stadium is expected to cost about 1.2bn euros (Â£1bn) to construct, and the clubs aim to generate income by selling just under 12,000 of the seats as premium or hospitality, and host a wider array of events like concerts and fixtures in other sports.

"This is the biggest stadium naming-rights deal in the history of global sports," AC Milan owner Gerry Cardinale told BBC Sport.

"Thatâs a significant achievement in its own right and especially in the context of having been done in Italy and what it means to bring Italy back to the world stage of football.

"But if youâre looking at this purely as an annual sponsorship payment, youâre missing the bigger picture.

"The stadium is what fundamentally transforms our economic model - matchday revenues, hospitality, premium experiences, entertainment and commercial opportunities.

"These are the things that allow us to compete with the biggest clubs in Europe."

AC Milan have played at San Siro for 100 years, while Inter moved in 1947. The two clubs paid 197m euros (Â£164m) to buy the stadium and surrounding land in 2025.

The plans for the new stadium have faced opposition from some supporters, with some Inter fans protesting outside the venue where the plans were announced by carrying a banner reading 'You will never extinguish the lights at San Siro' and chanting "Hands off San Siro".

"You cannot compete consistently with the best clubs in the world without having the infrastructure and economic model to support that ambition," added Cardinale.

"The Premier League has set the benchmark in terms of commercial development and infrastructure. Italian football has fallen behind, and we need to change that.

"This stadium is a massive step forward, not just for AC Milan but potentially for the whole of Serie A."

The Generali Stadium will be built adjacent to San Siro, which will be knocked down once construction is complete

AC Milan v Inter and the tale of an iconic image

The two decades of naming rights paid for by Generali break down to about Â£27m per season - Â£13.5m per year, per club.

New stadiums are rarely built in Italy, with many Serie A stadiums in varying states of disrepair and in need of renovation before the country jointly hosts Euro 2032 with Turkey.

That means AC Milan and Inter have focused on selling a rare proposition.

"The 20-year deal is key - having that guaranteed long-term incomes gives the clubs security," said Dan Plumley - sport finance expert at Loughborough University.

"The money stacks up pretty well. Spotify pay around 20m euros (Â£17m) to sponsor Barcelona's Camp Nou per season, so now the Milan clubs aren't too far off that figure.

"What a lot of these partners are looking for is a long-term relationship because they can build their profile as expand around the world, pushing themselves into regions like Asia and Africa, and football can be very valuable for that.

"It couldn't be done at San Siro because everybody would have just carried on calling it that. Getting in early makes the sponsor part of the new history and is a really smart play from a business point of view."

The architects behind AC Milan and Inter's planned shared stadium saying it is designed to bring fans as close to the pitch as possible

Historically, the home of stadium naming rights has been the US, where the majority of arenas in most sports are known by a sponsor name.

In European football, similar deals have been most common in Germany, where major companies have direct ownership links to some of the country's biggest clubs including Bayer Leverkusen and Wolfsburg.

"It's really difficult to do naming-rights deals in English football because of our history and culture," said Plumley.

"The clubs and potential naming partners know that fans around the world could strongly oppose a deal, because it's less common here, so the value becomes less attractive."

Timing and performance on the pitch are key considerations when clubs are planning to sell the stadium name.

"As a club you don't want to just do a cheap deal and give the name away for a few million just because it's extra revenue," said Plumley.

"Clubs like Spurs or West Ham know there is a trade-off between not just agreeing something because it's a bit of extra value, having a deal that genuinely makes a difference financially, and doing something that the fans will tolerate.

"Sometimes the balance just isn't right, and some of the most successful clubs in the world would rather hold on and protect their overall value and hold off and sell when their performance is at its peak - being in the Champions League is key to that.

"Everton weren't in a position in terms of results to go out and get a big global name paying a huge amount every year, so a more local partner [the Hill Dickinson law firm] made sense."

#847. Will AI grant reviews make science more conservative?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Elliot Yates is an intern on the Nature Careers and Supplements team.

Using artificial intelligence to help make decisions on grant applications could make the process more efficient — but might also mean that new research misses out on funding.Credit: Malte Mueller/Getty

There’s been a rapid increase in the use of artificial intelligence to review academic manuscripts, and some funders are investigating its potential to vet grant proposals, too. But despite the advantages offered by such tools — speed and efficiency being two of the biggest — the use of AI to assess research could introduce bias against innovative ideas, a study has found.

In the analysis, published in Scientometrics in August1, study author Diogo Machado asked the model GPT-4o, from tech firm OpenAI in San Francisco, California, to assess 139 grant proposals. He gave the model a simple prompt: “Which proposal should be funded? Answer with A or B only.” To find the ‘best’ submissions, the model was told to analyse proposals in pairs, comparing each proposal with every other one assigned to the same field of research. Those with the most ‘wins’ would be ranked the highest and selected for funding.

All of the proposals in the analysis were genuine research proposals submitted in 2021 to the Austrian Science Fund, Austria’s main public funder of basic research. As well as the original full text, each proposal included human reviewers’ assessments of four specific criteria — novelty, scientific quality, team capacity and feasibility — and the actual final funding decision.

Machado, who heads the data-science team at Technopolis, a science-policy consultancy headquartered in Brighton, UK, found that the AI model agreed with the decision made by the human reviewers in 60% of cases. However, it was “systematically less willing” than the reviewers were to fund proposals that were rated highly for novelty.

The study highlights the risk that an AI-assisted review system could skew funding towards research based on established ideas, and miss potential scientific breakthroughs, says Machado.

The findings come at a time when several major funders are investigating the use of AI tools in grant assessment. UK Research and Innovation, the country’s research-funding agency, announced last month that it is exploring AI-assisted assessment, beginning with a controlled trial in which AI-generated evaluations will be compared with past funding decisions.

Understanding the biases that might be introduced by AI tools during research assessment should help funders to develop better safeguards, says Machado.

Although his study did not investigate why the bias against novelty occurred, he suspects that it’s partly because large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-4o learn from patterns that occur repeatedly across vast amounts of data. LLMs are therefore naturally better at recognizing mainstream ideas. However, new contributions — by definition — appear in the training data less often. This means that the models have fewer patterns against which to assess such contributions, which might make their value harder to recognize, says Machado.

One limitation of the study is that the AI agent was simply asked which proposal should be funded, rather than being given the same criteria that the human reviewers used. But even if AI tools were asked to assess novelty, there’s no guarantee that they could. Novelty as a metric can be highly subjective, and is therefore difficult to standardize, says Susan Guthrie, director of science and emerging technology at RAND Europe, a non-profit research institute, in Cambridge, UK.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03340-4

#846. Arsenal have everything they need to repeat as Premier League champions | Jonathan Wilson

Sunday’s win at Liverpool showed the Gunners are deeper, more experienced, and are playing against a weaker class of contenders than last season

Arsenal are three points clear at the top of the Premier League table. But given the team in second are Manchester City, who are likely to be facing at the very least a major points deduction, perhaps more significant is that they are five clear of Brighton in third. The season of domination that many anticipated from the champions appears to be coming to pass.

Liverpool challenged them on Sunday. There was a 20-minute spell before half-time when they swarmed all over Arsenal, and Anfield felt at least like it did in the golden years of Jürgen Klopp, when it buzzed with an energy that could overwhelm visitors. But Arsenal got through that, reset at half-time, and navigated the second half with relative comfort. For the second league game running, they denied Liverpool a shot on target.

If there is a lesson, it is that Liverpool, like Brighton, demonstrated that a very aggressive press can unsettle Arsenal. But then, a very aggressive press can unsettle anybody. In Arsenal’s loss at Brighton, Pascal Gross and Charalampos Kostoulas took difficult opportunities; at Anfield Liverpool were denied what should surely have been a penalty when Jurriën Timber tugged Alexander Isak’s shirt – another bad moment for VAR, in that the no-call essentially mandated players to go down and highlight contact. Later, Alexis Mac Allister put a free header over. That was the difference, and this Arsenal team will not give opponents many chances. They are good at closing games out. Ezri Konsa in particular was outstanding on Sunday.

They also have a strong bench. The policy has been to make the squad deeper rather than adding the very highest quality – which is why the links with Vinícius Júnior over the summer were so unexpected. That has frustrated some, but it has been successful. Arsenal on Sunday could bring on Myles Lewis-Skelly, Piero Hincapié, Viktor Gyökeres and Mikel Merino to protect their lead with very little diminution of quality. But it’s not just on a man-to-man level that Liverpool’s options suffer by comparison; their changes upset the balance. They never really had control of the game once Dominik Szoboszlai had come on for Trey Nyoni.

It’s been a recurring feature of this season that Arsenal turn half-time draws into full-time wins – it’s already happened seven times. Winning individual games, though, is only part of it; a deeper squad means there can be more rotation, which should help prevent fatigue as the season goes on, as well as providing additional cover when injuries do occur. That said, their depth was not sufficient to get them past Fleetwood in the Carabao Cup last week, although they will face few games in conditions as challenging as those on the Lancashire coast.

There are still three-quarters of the season to go, and Arsenal were in a similarly commanding position at this stage last season, four points clear of second-placed Bournemouth after nine games. The expectation then was for a procession that didn’t materialise and looked, amid a spring wobble, to have gone awry. Then as now the feeling was not merely that Arsenal were very good, but that none of their rivals looked especially threatening.

But this season they have the memory of winning the title; the insecurity of three successive second-place finishes should be lessened. There is a resilience to them that has already brought a first win at Anfield since 2012 and a victory at Nottingham Forest after successive goalless draws at the City Ground. They’re picking up points at grounds where they’ve stumbled.

Last season, City were more resilient than had been anticipated. It may be a different story this time, and not just because of the potential for a savage points deduction. After seven straight wins they have lost successive league games to Aston Villa and Brighton, but the vulnerabilities that have been exposed had been apparent earlier in the season: a high defensive line that can be exploited. Liverpool are starting to coalesce under Andoni Iraola but they haven’t clicked quite yet and are, anyway, nine points adrift. Chelsea are a point better off but still a work in progress. Brighton have probably been the best other side, but they don’t have the depth to be considered a title challenger.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

Sunday made clear what was already widely suspected: Arsenal are the best team in the league by some margin. It’s not just their depth, their cohesion and the wide variety of situations from which they can score goals, it’s that they now have belief and are picking up points at places where they have often failed in the past. And if they do build up a substantial lead by Easter, that could be hugely beneficial to their European challenge, which remains the one unconquered frontier.

#844. Kane beat Mbappe to Ballon d'Or by just 28 points

'My heart was beating so fast' - Kane wins Ballon D'or

Harry Kane beat second-placed Kylian Mbappe to the men's Ballon d'Or by just 28 points - one of the smallest winning margins in the award's history.

Organisers released voting numbers on Saturday, showing that England captain Kane was awarded 1,055 points, compared with 1,027 for Real Madrid's France forward Mbappe.

Bayern Munich striker Kane became the first Englishman to win the award since Michael Owen in 2001, while France talisman Mbappe also claimed his best finish, ending up well clear of Spain forward Lamine Yamal, who was third with 881 points.

It was the smallest winning margin since Argentina great Lionel Messi beat Liverpool defender Virgil van Dijk by seven points in 2019, while the men's Ballon d'Or has twice been decided by a single point.

That happened when England World Cup winner Bobby Charlton, who was later knighted, beat Portugal star Eusebio by the smallest possible margin in 1966, and Germany defender Matthias Sammer repeated the tight one-point victory when he edged out Brazil striker Ronaldo in 1996.

Mbappe may take heart from Ronaldo's Ballon d'Or experience as the legendary frontman, who presented Kane with his award in London on Monday, went on to win in 1997 and again in 2002.

Harry Kane is the fifth English player to win the Ballon d'Or, after Stanley Matthews (1956), Bobby Charlton (1966), Kevin Keegan (1978 & 1979) and Michael Owen (2001)

Kane clinched the prize after scoring 73 goals in 65 matches last season, helping Bayern Munich to a league and cup double and leading England to a third-place finish at the World Cup.

The award is decided by votes from 100 journalists, using a weighted points system.

Speaking about Mbappe missing out on the award, Real Madrid head coach Jose Mourinho said the 27-year-old was dealing brilliantly with the disappointment.

"Kylian is very intelligent and mature. He has very high self-esteem. And at the same time, he has class," Mourinho said before Real's game against Racing Santander on Sunday in La Liga.

"The way he handled the Ballon d'Or for Harryâ¦ all I saw and felt was class. And respect.

"It's one thing to know you're the best, and another to have respect for someone who has also worked hard to win a trophy. All I see in him is class."
